Summary: Abolition is the movement to end slavery, driven in Britain and America largely by Christians convinced that every person bears God's image. Figures like William Wilberforce and Harriet Beecher Stowe argued from Scripture that owning people contradicts the gospel's claim that Christ died for all. The abolition story shows how biblical conviction, sustained over decades, can overturn even deeply entrenched injustice.

God does not give sparingly. From manna in the wilderness to loaves multiplied for a crowd, Scripture shows a Father who provides more than enough, and His generosity is meant to overflow into generosity toward others. Abundance is never about storing up for ourselves, but about trusting the Giver and sharing what He has given.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: To be accepted is to be welcomed as you are, and that is exactly how God receives those who come to Him through Christ. Jesus welcomed sinners, outcasts, and strangers, and Paul urges believers to accept one another just as Christ accepted them. Christian acceptance never means approving everything, but it does mean no one is beyond the reach of God's welcome.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Adam and Eve are the first humans in Genesis, created in God's image and placed in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. Their disobedience in eating the forbidden fruit brought sin and death into the world, yet God immediately promised a deliverer who would crush the serpent. Their story explains both human dignity and human brokenness, and why every person needs the second Adam, Jesus Christ.

Allegory is a way of reading a story in which characters and events stand for deeper spiritual realities beyond the literal sense. The Bible itself uses allegory at times, as when Paul treats Hagar and Sarah as pictures of two covenants, but allegory becomes dangerous when it replaces the plain meaning of the text. Used with restraint and anchored in the passage's own context, it can illuminate; untethered from context, it can make a text mean anything.

Ancient Israel was the covenant nation descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, called to be a light to the nations. Its history runs from the exodus and the giving of the Law through the monarchy, exile, and return, and it forms the setting for most of the Old Testament. Understanding ancient Israel — its worship, kings, prophets, and failures — is essential for reading the Bible as the story of God's redeeming work.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Angels are created spiritual beings who worship God, carry out His commands, and minister to His people. Scripture shows them as messengers, guardians, and warriors, yet always pointing attention to God rather than themselves. Believers respect angels biblically without worshiping them, rejoicing that they rejoice over every sinner who repents.
KeyPassages: Psalm 91:11; Psalm 103:20; Daniel 10; Luke 2:10-14; Hebrews 1:14; Hebrews 13:2; Revelation 22:8-9
RelatedDoctrines: Angels; Spiritual Warfare; Ministry of Angels
RelatedQuestions: Do people become angels when they die?; Do angels still appear today?

Summary: Anxiety is the troubled, divided mind Jesus tenderly addresses in the Sermon on the Mount, pointing anxious hearts to a Father who knows their needs and cares for sparrows and lilies. Scripture does not shame the anxious; it invites them to cast their cares on God in prayer and receive His peace. Christian hope gives anxiety an anchor: our future rests in God's hands, not our control.
KeyPassages: Psalm 94:19; Proverbs 12:25; Matthew 6:25-34; John 14:27; Philippians 4:6-7; 1 Peter 5:7
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible say about anxiety and worry?; Is anxiety a lack of faith?
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Proverbs; Matthew; John; Philippians; 1 Peter

Summary: Apologetics is the reasoned defense of the Christian faith, answering honest questions and giving reasons for hope. Peter urges believers to be ready with a gentle and respectful answer, and the New Testament itself models this in Paul's speeches and the apostles' appeal to eyewitness testimony. Good apologetics never replaces the gospel, but it clears away misunderstandings so the gospel can be heard.
RelatedQuestions: Is Jesus the only way to God?; Is the Bible reliable and true?

Summary: Apostasy is the sober reality of turning away from the faith once embraced. Scripture warns plainly that some will abandon the truth, exchanging it for error or for the world's approval, and it calls believers to hold fast and to watch over one another. The warnings are given not to frighten the faithful, but to keep them faithful.
RelatedPeople: Paul; John the Apostle; Judas Iscariot
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Kingdom Divides

Summary: Archaeology studies the material remains of the ancient world — cities, inscriptions, coins, and everyday objects — and it regularly illuminates the world of the Bible. Finds like the Cyrus Cylinder, the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Tel Dan inscription have confirmed names, places, and events once doubted. Archaeology cannot prove every claim of faith, but it anchors the biblical story in real history rather than myth.
RelatedQuestions: Is there archaeological evidence for King David?; What are the Dead Sea Scrolls?; Is there evidence for the Exodus?

Summary: Assurance is the settled confidence that a person who trusts in Christ truly belongs to God and will be kept by Him. It rests not on the strength of our feelings but on God's promises, Christ's finished work, and the Spirit's witness in the heart. Doubt does not necessarily mean unbelief; assurance grows as believers look away from themselves and toward Jesus.
RelatedQuestions: How can I know I am truly saved?; Can I lose my salvation?

Summary: Atonement is Christ's work on the cross reconciling sinners to a holy God, bearing the penalty our sin deserved. Old Testament sacrifices pictured it for centuries, but only Jesus' once-for-all offering truly takes away sin. Because of the atonement, believers can draw near to God with confidence and peace.
KeyPassages: Leviticus 16; Isaiah 53:4-6; Romans 3:25; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 9:22-28; 1 John 2:2
RelatedPeople: Aaron; Isaiah; Jesus; John the Baptist; Paul
RelatedQuestions: Why did Jesus have to die for our sins?; What does atonement mean?

Summary: Authority in the Christian life asks who gets to say what is true and right: God, speaking in Scripture, holds ultimate authority over conscience and church. Human authorities — parents, rulers, pastors — deserve honor, but their authority is delegated and limited, never absolute. When human commands contradict God's word, believers obey God rather than people, and they do so with respect rather than rebellion.

Baptism is the public sign Jesus gave His church marking a believer's union with Him in His death and resurrection and their entry into His people. Going under the water pictures being washed clean; rising pictures new life in Christ. Baptism does not save by itself, but it joyfully obeys the Savior who saves.
KeyPassages: Matthew 3:13-17; Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38-41; Acts 8:36-38; Romans 6:3-4; Colossians 2:12; 1 Peter 3:21
RelatedPeople: Jesus; John the Baptist; Peter; Philip; Paul
RelatedQuestions: Why do Christians get baptized?; Should babies be baptized?

Summary: Beauty is a gift from the Creator, woven into the world from the first sunrise to the craftsmanship of the tabernacle. Scripture treats beauty as something to enjoy with gratitude, not to worship, and as a pointer to the glory of the God who made it. The Christian vision of beauty reaches its height in Christ, whose character is beautiful even in suffering, and in the new creation where all things will be made lovely.

Belief is more than agreeing with an idea; it is trusting a Person. Scripture calls us to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and to stake our lives on that truth. Such belief receives forgiveness, gives new life, and shows itself in obedience.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: Long before Jesus was born, Micah promised that a ruler would come from little Bethlehem, one whose origins are from ancient days. Matthew sees that promise fulfilled when Jesus is born in David's town, the shepherd-king who would rule not by force but by laying down His life. The smallness of Bethlehem is the point: God's greatest King came in the humblest way.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary

Summary: The Bible is the collection of sixty-six books, written over many centuries, that Christians receive as God's word in human words. It tells one unfolding story — creation, fall, redemption, and new creation — with Jesus Christ at its center. Christians read it to know God, to be shaped by His truth, and to find their place in His purposes.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture
RelatedQuestions: Is the Bible reliable and true?; Who wrote the Bible?; How should I start reading the Bible?

Summary: Bible history is the true story the Scriptures tell, from creation through the patriarchs, Israel, Jesus, and the early church. Because the Bible's claims are rooted in events that happened in real places at real times, its history can be studied, questioned, and tested like any history. Knowing the sweep of that story helps readers see how each passage fits into God's larger work of redemption.
RelatedQuestions: How did the world begin according to Genesis?; What was the Exodus from Egypt?

Summary: Bible reliability asks whether the Scriptures we have today faithfully preserve what was originally written, and whether their claims about history hold up. The manuscript evidence for the New Testament is vast, the Old Testament was copied with extraordinary care, and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed biblical details. Reliability does not remove the need for faith, but it means faith in the Bible is not blind.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture
RelatedQuestions: Is the Bible reliable and true?; Has the Bible been changed over time?; Why are there so many Bible translations?

Summary: Biblical authority is the conviction that Scripture, as God's breathed-out word, is the final court of appeal for belief and behavior. It does not mean every question has a proof text, but it does mean that where Scripture speaks clearly, Christians submit even when culture disagrees. This authority is exercised humbly, through careful interpretation in community, not as a weapon for private agendas.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: Biblical interpretation is the careful work of understanding what a passage meant to its first readers so it can be applied faithfully today. It attends to context, genre, language, and the whole sweep of Scripture, resisting both wooden literalism and fanciful speculation. Good interpretation is a community task, tested by the church across time, and its goal is not mastery of the text but obedience to the God who speaks through it.

Blessing is God's favor resting on His people, spoken over Abraham and extended to every nation through Christ. In the Old Testament it meant land, children, and God's presence; in the New Testament it reaches its fullness as every spiritual blessing in Christ. To be blessed is to live under God's kind hand, and to become a blessing to others.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: At the threshold of the Promised Land, Moses set before Israel two paths: blessing for obedience and curse for rebellion. The choice was stark because the covenant was serious — God's people could not drift into faithfulness. Yet the story does not end with curse, for Christ bore the curse so that the blessing of Abraham might come to all who believe.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Crossing the Jordan

Summary: Boldness is the Spirit-given courage to speak and act for Christ even when it costs something. The early church prayed not for safety but for boldness, and Peter and John, once fearful, spoke openly before the very council that had condemned Jesus. Christian boldness is never arrogance; it pairs truth with love and rests on the conviction that God is with His people.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Paul

Summary: Bread is God's daily provision, from manna in the wilderness to the prayer 'give us this day our daily bread.' Jesus multiplied loaves for hungry crowds and then declared, 'I am the Bread of Life,' giving His own body as food for the world. At His table we remember Him and are nourished by grace until He comes again.
KeyPassages: Exodus 16:4; Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 6:11; John 6:35; John 6:51; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Feeding of the Five Thousand; The Last Supper

Summary: Believers are not merely like-minded individuals; they are brothers and sisters, bound together as one family in Christ. Scripture urges them to love one another warmly, carry one another's burdens, and live at peace. True brotherhood shows the world what the Father's household looks like.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; John the Apostle; Joseph, Son of Jacob

Summary: Buddhism is the tradition founded on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, which diagnoses human suffering as the fruit of craving and prescribes the Eightfold Path toward release. Christians can appreciate Buddhism's seriousness about suffering and self-discipline while disagreeing at decisive points: the Bible teaches a personal Creator, the reality of the self, and salvation by grace through Christ rather than by self-effort. Fair engagement means describing Buddhism as its followers understand it, then presenting Jesus with grace.

Calling is God's summons on a person's life — first the general call to follow Christ, then the particular work He gives each believer to do. Every legitimate vocation can be a calling when done for God's glory, whether preaching, farming, parenting, or healing. Discerning a calling takes time, counsel, and attention to gifts, needs, and open doors, and it is tested by faithfulness more than by feelings of certainty.

The canon is the recognized list of books that make up the Bible, settled by the early church's recognition of apostolic and prophetic writings rather than by arbitrary decree. Christians believe the church discerned the canon under God's guidance, receiving books that bore the marks of divine authority and widespread use. Questions about disputed books are best answered by history: which writings did the earliest Christians treat as Scripture?

Character is who you are when no one is watching, and God shapes it slowly through trials, obedience, and time. Scripture links suffering to endurance, endurance to character, and character to hope. The goal is not a polished reputation but a life that quietly resembles Christ.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Christ alone saves, because He alone is both God and man, both priest and sacrifice. No teacher, ritual, or good deed can stand beside Him; to add anything to Christ is to lose Christ. The church confesses Him as the only mediator between God and humanity, and the only name by which we are saved.

Jesus did not only teach the way; He walked it. He washed feet, welcomed children, forgave enemies, and laid down His life, leaving His followers a pattern to follow. To follow His example is not to earn salvation but to live out the salvation He has given.

The New Testament ends with a promise: Jesus will return, visibly and gloriously, to judge the world and make all things new. His first coming was in humility; His second will be in power, and every believer is called to live ready — watchful, faithful, and full of hope.

Christian ethics asks how followers of Jesus should live, grounding right and wrong in God's character and commands rather than in shifting opinion. The Ten Commandments, the Sermon on the Mount, and the call to love neighbor give shape to decisions about money, work, speech, sexuality, and power. Christian ethics is not mere rule-keeping; it flows from a heart renewed by grace and aims at human flourishing under God.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: The Christian life is the whole of life lived in response to the gospel: trusting Christ, turning from sin, and growing in love for God and neighbor. It is ordinary as often as it is dramatic — work done honestly, meals shared, prayers whispered, forgiveness extended — and it is sustained by the church, the Scriptures, and the Spirit. Growth is rarely linear, but its direction is clear: becoming more like Jesus.
RelatedQuestions: How can I grow spiritually?

Summary: Christian living is ordinary life offered to God: work, family, neighbors, and rest all shaped by the gospel. Paul sums it up as presenting our bodies as living sacrifices and being transformed by renewed minds. It is not perfection but direction — a life increasingly conformed to Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: Christian witness is the task of making Jesus known through words and life, so that others can see and hear the gospel. It combines clear testimony about what Christ has done with a life that makes that testimony believable, and it is carried out with gentleness and respect. Every believer is a witness, whether by speaking to a friend, serving a neighbor, or standing firm under pressure.
RelatedQuestions: How can I share my faith with others?

Summary: Christology is the study of who Jesus Christ is: fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. The early church defended this against errors that made Jesus merely human or merely divine, because only a Savior who is both can bridge the gap between God and humanity. Christology matters practically: the Jesus we worship must be great enough to save and near enough to sympathize with our weakness.
RelatedQuestions: Who is Jesus Christ?

Summary: The church is God's people called out from the world, united to Christ as His body and bride, and gathered in local congregations for worship, teaching, fellowship, and mission. It is not a building or an event but a family God is building across every nation and century. Despite its flaws, Christ loves the church and gave Himself for her.
KeyPassages: Matthew 16:18; Acts 2:42-47; 1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 2:19-22; Ephesians 5:25; 1 Peter 2:9
RelatedQuestions: Why do I need to go to church if I believe in Jesus?; What is the church supposed to do?

Summary: Church councils were gatherings of Christian leaders who settled disputes about doctrine and practice, most famously at Nicaea in 325 and Chalcedon in 451. Their creeds — affirming that Christ is truly God and truly man — still shape what Christians confess today. Councils were not perfect, and their authority rests on their faithfulness to Scripture, but they show how the church has guarded the gospel together across generations.

The church grows as the gospel spreads and believers are added to the fellowship. Acts shows growth through preaching, prayer, shared life, and suffering, never through human technique alone. Healthy growth is both numerical and spiritual: more disciples, and deeper ones.

Church history traces the people of God from Pentecost to the present: through persecution, councils, missions, reformations, and revivals. It is a story of remarkable faithfulness and sobering failure, and knowing it guards Christians against both arrogance and despair. The same gospel that sustained martyrs and missionaries is the gospel the church carries today.

Church hurt is the pain caused when God's people wound one another — through harsh leadership, betrayal, exclusion, or hypocrisy. Scripture does not minimize such wounds: Jesus warned sternly about those who harm His little ones, and the Psalms give voice to grief over betrayal by close companions. Healing often involves honest lament, wise counsel, boundaries where needed, and, in time, the hard work of forgiveness — without pretending the hurt did not happen.

God is a God of order, and the church reflects His character when its life is ordered well — leaders qualified, worship decent, disputes handled with wisdom. Order is not cold bureaucracy; it is love given structure, so that the whole body can flourish and the gospel is not hindered.

Comfort is the consolation God gives His people in trouble, not by removing every sorrow but by His presence within it. Paul calls God the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us so that we can comfort others. Christian comfort is honest about pain and confident about hope, pointing sufferers to a Savior who wept and to a future without tears.

When Judah faced exile, Isaiah spoke comfort: her warfare is ended, her iniquity pardoned, and her God is coming. Comfort for Judah was never mere sympathy; it was the promise that God had not abandoned His people and would bring them home. That same comfort reaches all who mourn under judgment, pointing to Christ who bears our sorrows.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Israel waited for a King who would reign in righteousness, and the prophets pictured Him riding humbly into Jerusalem. Jesus entered the city to acclaim, yet His crown would be thorns before it was glory. He is the Coming King who will return to reign forever, and His kingdom is already breaking into the world.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; King David; Zechariah the Prophet

Summary: Communion, or the Lord's Supper, is the meal Jesus instituted on the night before His death, in which believers eat bread and drink wine in remembrance of Him. Churches differ on exactly how Christ is present in the meal, but all agree it proclaims His death, nourishes faith, and binds believers to one another. It is both a backward look to the cross and a forward look to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
RelatedQuestions: What is baptism and should I be baptized?

Summary: Community is the shared life of God's people, who are called not merely to believe the same things but to belong to one another. The early church shared meals, possessions, prayers, and burdens, and the New Testament's one-another commands assume Christians live in close, committed fellowship. In a lonely age, the church's community is itself a witness to a gospel that makes strangers into family.
RelatedQuestions: Why should I go to church?

Summary: Compassion is love that sees suffering and moves toward it, as Jesus did when He wept, touched the untouchable, and fed the hungry. It is more than feeling sorry; it acts, even at cost, and it reflects the heart of a God who is full of compassion. Christians practice compassion in hospitals and homes, in generosity and advocacy, knowing they themselves have received mercy.
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: God's compassion does not stop at Israel's borders. Jonah learned this reluctantly when God spared Nineveh, and Isaiah foresaw a Servant who would be a light to the nations. In Christ, that compassion reaches every tribe and tongue, and the church carries it to the ends of the earth.

Confession is the honest naming of sin before God and, where fitting, before others, trusting His promise to forgive and cleanse. It is not groveling but agreement with the truth, and it restores fellowship that sin has broken. The church has long practiced confession both privately and together, because sins hidden tend to grow, while sins confessed lose their power.

The conquest of Canaan was God's gift of the land He had promised, won not by Israel's strength but by His presence. Yet the conquest was incomplete, and the land itself pointed forward to a greater rest. The battles remind us that God's promises are sure, and that victory belongs to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: Crossing the Jordan; The Walls of Jericho

Summary: Conscience is the inner witness that accuses or excuses us, a gift of God that can be trained, dulled, or misled. Paul speaks of a clear conscience and a weak conscience, urging believers to inform conscience by Scripture and to respect the consciences of others. A conscience captive to God's word is a guide to freedom, not a tyrant of guilt.

To be consecrated is to be set apart for God's purposes, as Israel was called a holy nation and believers are called a holy priesthood. Consecration touches every part of life — body, work, worship — offered wholly to God. It is not withdrawal from the world but dedication within it.

Jude urges believers to contend for the faith once delivered, not with cruelty but with conviction. False teaching spreads quietly, so the church must know the truth well enough to recognize its counterfeits. Contending is an act of love: for God, for the church, and for those being led astray.
RelatedPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle

Summary: Contentment is the quiet sufficiency that comes from trusting God's provision rather than chasing more. Paul learned it in plenty and in want, and Hebrews ties it to God's promise never to leave or forsake His people. Contentment is not passivity or the denial of ambition; it is freedom from the tyranny of comparison and craving.

Context is the setting that gives a passage its meaning: the surrounding verses, the whole book, the author's world, and the sweep of Scripture. Ignoring context is the surest way to misuse the Bible, turning promises into slogans and commands into weapons. Careful readers ask what a text meant before asking what it means, and let the clear passages interpret the obscure ones.

Conversion is the turning of a person from sin and self-rule to God through repentance and faith in Christ. It may be sudden, like Paul's on the Damascus road, or gradual, like a slow dawn, but its marks are consistent: a new allegiance, a new direction, and a new life. Conversion is God's work from first to last, and it is the doorway into the Christian life, not its finish line.

Courage is the strength to do what is right when fear says otherwise, and Scripture ties it to God's presence rather than to personality. Joshua was told to be strong and courageous because God would be with him, and Esther risked her life with the words, if I perish, I perish. Christian courage is not the absence of fear but obedience in spite of it.
RelatedPeople: Joshua; Queen Esther; Daniel; Simon Peter
RelatedEvents: Esther Saves Her People; David and Goliath

Summary: A covenant is God's solemn, binding promise to His people, sealed in love and faithfulness. From Noah and Abraham to the new covenant in Christ's blood, covenants trace God's steady plan to dwell with His people. Every covenant points forward to Jesus, in whom all God's promises find their Yes.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15; Genesis 17:1-8; Exodus 19:5-6; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13
RelatedPeople: Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Jeremiah; Jesus
RelatedDoctrines: Covenant; New Covenant; Faithfulness of God
RelatedQuestions: What is a covenant in the Bible?; How is the new covenant different from the old?
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Jeremiah; Luke; Hebrews; 2 Samuel
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Davidic Covenant; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: Covenant love is God's steadfast, loyal love — the Hebrew hesed — that keeps His promises even when His people break theirs. It is love bound by oath, shown at Sinai, renewed through the prophets, and poured out fully in Christ. To know covenant love is to rest in a faithfulness that never lets go.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: Again and again God's people returned to renew their covenant: at Shechem under Joshua, under Josiah after the Law was found, and under Nehemiah after exile. Renewal meant hearing God's word, confessing failure, and recommitting to obey. Every generation needs its own renewal, for faith is never inherited automatically.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: Israel's story is shadowed by unfaithfulness — idols, injustice, and forgotten vows. The prophets name it plainly: the people broke the covenant their God had kept. Yet even unfaithfulness becomes a stage for grace, as God disciplines, restores, and finally keeps the covenant Himself in Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Kingdom Divides

Summary: Creation is God's free act of making all things out of nothing by His word, declaring them good, and sustaining them by His power. It reveals His glory, wisdom, and kindness, and gives human beings, made in His image, both dignity and purpose. Caring for creation and marveling at it are fitting responses to a Creator who still upholds every star and sparrow.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:1; Genesis 1:27; Psalm 19:1; John 1:3; Colossians 1:16-17; Hebrews 11:3; Revelation 4:11
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?; What does it mean to be made in the image of God?

Summary: Creeds are short, shared statements of faith — like the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed — that summarize what Christians believe about God, Christ, and salvation. They arose to guard the gospel against error and to give believers words to confess together. Creeds do not replace Scripture, but they help the church recognize faithful teaching and pass it on intact.

The cross is the centre of the Christian faith, where Jesus bore our sin, defeated the powers of evil, and reconciled us to God. What looked like shame and defeat, God turned into wisdom, power, and salvation for all who believe. Believers take up their cross daily, boasting only in the cross of Christ.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 53:4-6; Matthew 27:32-56; John 19:17-30; 1 Corinthians 1:18; Galatians 6:14; Colossians 2:14-15
RelatedBooks: Isaiah; Matthew; John; 1 Corinthians; Galatians; Colossians
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Paul

Summary: The crucifixion is the execution of Jesus on a Roman cross outside Jerusalem, the event at the center of the Christian faith. The Gospels describe it in stark detail — the mockery, the darkness, the cry of dereliction, the final breath — and the apostles proclaim its meaning: Christ died for our sins, bearing the curse in our place. The cross is both history's darkest hour and the source of the world's hope.
RelatedQuestions: Why did Jesus have to die on the cross?

Summary: Culture is the shared way of life of a people — its stories, customs, arts, and values — and Christians live within cultures without simply absorbing them. The gospel judges every culture, affirming what is good and true in it while challenging what contradicts God's word. Faithful cultural engagement means neither withdrawal nor conformity, but discerning participation for the common good.

Judges tells a grim cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and sin again. Each round shows that Israel's problem was not bad leaders but a wandering heart. The cycle only breaks when a true King comes who can change hearts from within.
RelatedEvents: Deborah and Barak Defeat Sisera; Gideon's Victory over Midian

Summary: Faith is not only for crises; it is for Tuesday mornings. Daily faith means trusting God for today's bread, today's work, and today's obedience, one day at a time. The manna principle still holds: God gives enough for today, and tomorrow's grace arrives tomorrow.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Wilderness Wanderings

Summary: Darkness in Scripture pictures ignorance, evil, and separation from God, set against the light of His presence and truth. The world loved darkness rather than light, John writes, yet into that darkness the true Light has come. Darkness is real and terrible, but it is not ultimate: it cannot overcome the light, and one day night itself will be no more.

From Ruth and Boaz through Jesse to David, and from David to Jesus, Scripture traces a family line held together by God's promise. The lineage includes outsiders, failures, and kings, showing that God's plan runs through real human history. Matthew opens his Gospel with this genealogy to announce: the promised King has arrived.

God promised David a house, a throne, and a kingdom that would last forever. David's sons failed, but the promise did not, for it pointed beyond them to a Son of David who would reign eternally. In Jesus, the Davidic covenant finds its fulfillment and its King.

The Day of the Lord is the day God steps in decisively — to judge evil, rescue His people, and set the world right. The prophets warned that it would be darkness for the proud and light for the humble, and the New Testament ties it to Christ's return. It is both a warning to the complacent and a hope for the oppressed.

Death entered the world through sin, and Scripture treats it with sober honesty: it is an enemy, the last enemy, not a natural friend. Yet for those in Christ, death has lost its sting, because Jesus died and rose again, and believers who die fall asleep in Him awaiting resurrection. Grief remains real, but it is grief with hope.

Definitions matter in theology because words like grace, faith, and love carry precise biblical meanings that popular use often blurs. Careful definition guards against misunderstanding: grace is not permission to sin, faith is not wishful thinking, and love is not mere sentiment. The church defines its terms by Scripture's own usage, in community across time, so that believers can speak truth clearly to one another and to the world.

Deliverance is God's rescue of His people from bondage, danger, or oppression, supremely in the exodus from Egypt and ultimately in Christ's victory over sin and death. The pattern repeats across Scripture: God hears cries, acts with a mighty hand, and leads His people into freedom. Deliverance reminds believers that salvation is God's work, not human achievement, and that He still rescues today.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: God heard Israel's groaning in Egypt and delivered them with a mighty hand through Moses, the Passover, and the parting of the sea. The Exodus became Israel's defining story of salvation, retold at every Passover. The New Testament presents Jesus' work as the greater Exodus, delivering us from slavery to sin and death.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Passover; The Crucifixion

Summary: Dependence is not weakness to be outgrown but the truth of the Christian life: apart from Christ we can do nothing. Like branches on a vine, believers draw every good thing from Him — strength, wisdom, and fruit. To depend on God is to live honestly, admitting need and receiving grace.
RelatedEvents: The Temptation in the Wilderness; Jesus Prays in Gethsemane

Summary: Desire is the longing of the heart, which God made good but sin has twisted toward forbidden objects. Scripture distinguishes desires that lead to life — hunger for God, for righteousness, for communion — from cravings that enslave. The Christian task is not to kill desire but to retrain it, delighting in God above all so that lesser desires find their proper place.

Devotion is the steady, loving attention of the heart to God, expressed in prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience. Mary sitting at Jesus' feet pictures devotion better than any definition: presence before performance, listening before doing. Devotion is not measured by intensity of feeling but by faithfulness over time, returning to God again and again.

Dignity is the worth every person carries as one made in God's image, regardless of age, ability, status, or usefulness. It grounds the Christian defense of the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, and the stranger: no one is disposable because no one is an accident. Honoring dignity means treating every person as someone for whom Christ died.

Diligence is steady, faithful effort over the long haul — the ant's wisdom, the athlete's discipline, the farmer's patience. Scripture warns against laziness and praises the worker who keeps at the task God has given. Diligence trusts that small, faithful acts compound into a life well lived.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Work was given before the Fall, not as punishment but as purpose: to tend, build, and create. Scripture calls believers to work heartily, as for the Lord, whether in fields, workshops, or homes. Diligent work honors God, serves neighbors, and witnesses to a faith that takes ordinary life seriously.
RelatedPeople: Adam; Paul; Joseph, Son of Jacob

Summary: Discernment is the Spirit-shaped ability to distinguish truth from error and good from merely plausible. It grows through Scripture, prayer, community, and experience, and it is needed most where falsehood wears a disguise — in teaching, in guidance, and in cultural pressures. Discernment is humble: it tests everything, holds fast to what is good, and admits it can be wrong.
RelatedPeople: King Solomon; Paul; John the Apostle

Summary: Discipleship is following Jesus daily, learning from His word, obeying His commands, and helping others do the same. It is more than believing facts about Christ; it is a whole life reordered around Him, whatever the cost. The Great Commission makes disciple-making the normal mission of every believer, not just church leaders.
KeyPassages: Matthew 4:19; Matthew 28:18-20; Luke 9:23; John 15:8; Acts 2:42; 2 Timothy 2:2
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Peter; Andrew; Paul; Timothy; Barnabas
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean to be a disciple of Jesus?; How do I disciple someone else?

Summary: Divinity refers to the nature of being God: eternal, self-existent, all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly holy. Christians confess one God whose divinity is shared fully by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and they insist that Jesus possesses true divinity, not a lesser or borrowed kind. To speak of divinity is to speak of the One before whom all worship and obedience are due.

Doctrine is teaching about God and His ways, drawn from Scripture and summarized for the church's belief and life. Good doctrine is not dry theory: what Christians believe about God shapes how they pray, suffer, forgive, and hope. The church tests doctrine by Scripture, and holds it with both conviction and humility, knowing that God is greater than any human summary of Him.

Doubt is the unsettled questioning many honest believers face about God's goodness, truth, or presence, and Scripture treats doubters with surprising tenderness. From the Psalms to Thomas to John the Baptist in prison, God's people have wrestled and been met with evidence and mercy. Doubt need not be the end of faith; handled honestly, it can deepen it.
RelatedPeople: Thomas; John the Baptist; Gideon; Asaph
RelatedQuestions: Is it a sin to doubt God?; What should I do when my faith feels weak?

Summary: God sometimes spoke through dreams — to Joseph in Egypt, to Daniel in Babylon, to Joseph the carpenter in Bethlehem. Dreams in Scripture are never treated as private horoscopes; they are tested by God's word and often carry His guidance for others. They remind us that God speaks in ways we do not control, and His messages always serve His purposes.
RelatedPeople: Joseph, Son of Jacob; Daniel; Joseph, Husband of Mary

Summary: In a valley of dry bones, God asked Ezekiel whether they could live, then breathed life into them by His Spirit. The vision promised Israel's restoration from exile, and it points further to resurrection itself: the God who revives the dead can revive any hopeless situation. No valley is too dry for His breath.

The early church is the community born at Pentecost, when the Spirit empowered frightened disciples to preach Christ boldly. Its life — teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayer, and mission — became the pattern for churches ever since, and its spread from Jerusalem to Rome shows the gospel crossing every barrier. The early church was far from perfect, but its courage and love remain a challenge to every generation.

Easter is the celebration of Jesus' resurrection from the dead on the third day after His crucifixion, the event that vindicated His claims and defeated death. The empty tomb and the risen Lord's appearances turned despairing disciples into witnesses willing to die for what they had seen. Easter is not only a day but the pattern of Christian hope: suffering is real, but it does not have the last word.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Simon Peter; Paul
RelatedQuestions: Did Jesus really rise from the dead?

Summary: Emotions are part of God's good design, not enemies of faith: the Psalms give voice to joy, anger, fear, grief, and longing, and Jesus Himself wept and rejoiced. Emotions inform us but do not rule us; mature faith feels deeply while testing feelings against truth. The goal is not stoic numbness but emotions ordered by love for God and neighbor.

Encouragement is a ministry every believer can practice: strengthening hearts, cheering the weary, and reminding one another of God's promises. Barnabas earned the name 'son of encouragement' by standing with new believers and vouching for the unlikely. A word of encouragement can be the difference between quitting and enduring.

The end times describe the last chapter of history: Christ's return, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and the new heaven and new earth. Christians disagree on details and timelines, but agree on the essentials: Jesus will return bodily, evil will be judged, and God's people will live with Him forever. The proper response to end-times teaching is watchful hope, not fearful speculation.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Jesus; Paul; John the Apostle
RelatedQuestions: Will Jesus come back?; What are the signs of the end times?

Summary: Endurance is staying faithful when faith is costly — under trial, persecution, or long waiting. Hebrews pictures believers surrounded by witnesses, laying aside weights and looking to Jesus, who endured the cross. Endurance is not grim stoicism but hope-fueled perseverance to the finish.
RelatedPeople: Paul; James, Son of Zebedee; Stephen

Summary: God's gifts are meant to be enjoyed, not merely endured: food, friendship, beauty, rest, and laughter are given by a generous Father. Scripture warns against both idolatry and ingratitude, teaching us to receive good things with thanks and open hands. Enjoyment with thanksgiving is itself a form of worship.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Eschatology is the study of last things: death, judgment, heaven, hell, Christ's return, and the renewal of all things. It reminds believers that history is going somewhere and that present suffering is not the end of the story. Different traditions order these events differently, but all Christian eschatology ends in hope: God will dwell with His people and wipe away every tear.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle

Summary: Eternal life is not merely life that goes on forever, but life in knowing God through Jesus Christ, begun now and completed in the resurrection. It is a gift, not a wage, received by faith and sealed by the Spirit. Eternal life transforms the present — freeing believers from the fear of death — and it will one day mean embodied life in a renewed creation.

Eternal security is the conviction that those truly united to Christ cannot finally be lost, because their keeping depends on God's faithfulness rather than their own grip. Jesus promised that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand, and Paul traced salvation from predestination to glorification without a break. This assurance is meant to produce humility and holiness, not carelessness, since those who persist in sin give reason to question whether they ever truly believed.
RelatedQuestions: Can I lose my salvation?; How can I know I am truly saved?

Summary: Eternity is God's own mode of existence: without beginning or end, unbound by time as creatures know it. Scripture contrasts God's eternity with human brevity — a thousand years are like a day to Him — and promises believers a share in His unending life. Eternity is not endless boredom but endless fullness, life in the presence of the God who is Himself infinite.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Isaiah; Simon Peter; John the Apostle

Summary: Ethics is the study of right and wrong, and Christian ethics roots moral judgment in God's character revealed in Scripture. It asks not only what rules to follow but what kind of people to become: truthful, just, merciful, and pure. In a world of competing moral visions, Christian ethics offers both clarity about God's commands and grace for those who fail to keep them.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Evangelism is sharing the good news of Jesus Christ with others and calling them to repent and believe. It flows from gratitude for God's grace and compassion for people who are lost, and God uses ordinary believers' words and lives to draw people to Himself. The message is Christ crucified and risen; the power belongs to God, the privilege to us.
KeyPassages: Matthew 28:18-20; Mark 16:15; Acts 1:8; Acts 8:35; Romans 10:14-15; 2 Corinthians 5:20; 1 Peter 3:15
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?; What exactly is the gospel I should share?

Summary: Evidence in the Christian faith includes historical testimony, manuscript data, fulfilled prophecy, transformed lives, and the coherence of the gospel's picture of the world. Christians do not claim proof that compels belief against the will, but they do claim that faith is reasonable and that honest investigation has good grounds to proceed. The strongest evidence, the apostles insisted, is the resurrection of Jesus, attested by eyewitnesses.
RelatedQuestions: Is the Bible reliable and true?; Did Jesus really rise from the dead?

Summary: Evil and suffering are the hardest challenge to faith in a good and powerful God, and Scripture meets it with honesty rather than easy answers. The Bible shows a world broken by sin, a God who enters suffering in Christ, and a promise that evil will one day be judged and undone. Christians do not claim to explain every instance of pain, but they trust a God who suffered Himself and who will make all things new.
RelatedQuestions: Why does God allow suffering?; Why does God seem silent in my hardest seasons?

Summary: Evolution is the scientific account of how life diversified over time, and Christians differ on how it relates to Genesis. Some read Genesis as teaching a recent six-day creation, others as teaching God's purposeful creation in language that accommodates ancient understanding, and still others hold intermediate views. What all orthodox Christians affirm together is that God is the Creator, that humans bear His image, and that Adam's fall is real history with real consequences.
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?; How did the world begin according to Genesis?

Summary: The Exile is God's judgment on unfaithful Judah, when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and carried the people far from home. Far from being the end of the story, exile became a season of refining, fresh revelation, and longing for restoration. God kept a remnant, brought His people home, and pointed them to a greater return in Christ.
KeyPassages: 2 Kings 25; Psalm 137:1; Jeremiah 29:11; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Daniel 1; Ezra 1:1-4
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; Ezra; Nehemiah; Cyrus
RelatedQuestions: Why did God send Israel into exile?; What can Christians learn from the exile?
RelatedBooks: 2 Kings; Psalms; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; Ezra
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Because of persistent idolatry, Israel and Judah were carried into exile, losing land, temple, and king, yet God did not abandon them there. Prophets like Jeremiah and Ezekiel spoke hope in exile, and under Cyrus God brought His people home to rebuild. The return was real but incomplete, pointing forward to the greater restoration Jesus brings.
KeyPassages: 2 Kings 25:21; Jeremiah 29:4-14; Ezekiel 37:1-14; Ezra 1:1-4; Psalm 137:1; Isaiah 40:1-11
RelatedBooks: 2 Kings; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Ezra; Psalms; Isaiah
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Daniel; Ezra; Nehemiah; Cyrus the Great
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: The existence of God is the question of whether a Creator lies behind the universe, and Christians point to several lines of evidence: the beginning and fine-tuning of the cosmos, the reality of objective moral values, the human hunger for meaning, and the historical person of Jesus. The Bible itself treats God's existence as evident from creation, so that unbelief is a moral as well as intellectual matter. Arguments can open doors, but knowing God comes through Christ.

The Exodus is Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt through the Red Sea under Moses, the defining Old Testament picture of redemption. Through plagues, Passover, and the covenant at Sinai, God showed He keeps His promises and dwells with His people. The New Testament reads the Exodus as a foreshadowing of the greater deliverance Jesus brings from sin.
KeyPassages: Exodus 3:7-10; Exodus 12:13; Exodus 14:13-14; Exodus 20:2; Deuteronomy 7:8; 1 Corinthians 10:1-4
RelatedQuestions: Did the Exodus really happen?; How does the Exodus point to Jesus?
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; The Passover; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Commandments

Summary: Eyewitnesses are central to the Christian claim, because the apostles presented themselves not as philosophers but as witnesses to events they had seen and heard. Luke researched eyewitness accounts, Paul listed resurrection witnesses many still living, and John insisted he wrote what his eyes had seen and his hands had touched. The faith stands or falls on whether these witnesses told the truth, which is why their willingness to suffer for it matters.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; Paul; John the Apostle
RelatedQuestions: Did Jesus really rise from the dead?

Summary: Faith is trust in God and His promises, receiving Christ and resting on Him alone for salvation. It is a gift of God that unites believers to Jesus and inevitably produces love, obedience, and endurance. The heroes of Hebrews 11 show that faith sees the unseen and acts on God's word even when circumstances argue otherwise.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 10:17; Ephesians 2:8; Hebrews 11:1; Hebrews 11:6; James 2:17
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Rahab; Moses; Paul; Jesus; Noah; Mary
RelatedQuestions: What is faith according to the Bible?; Can faith and doubt exist together?
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Habakkuk; Romans; Ephesians; Hebrews; James
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; Noah and the Flood; The Resurrection

Summary: Faith and reason are allies, not enemies, in the Christian vision: faith trusts what God has revealed, and reason helps us understand, defend, and apply it. The greatest Christian thinkers have used philosophy, logic, and evidence in service of the gospel, while insisting that reason is a servant, not a master, and that some truths exceed what unaided reason can reach. A faith that fears questions is fragile; a faith that welcomes them grows stronger.

Faithfulness is loyalty over time — keeping promises when it costs, trusting God when He seems silent, and doing the next right thing. Scripture celebrates it in Daniel, Joseph, and countless unnamed saints, and above all in God Himself, whose faithfulness never fails. To be faithful is to mirror the character of the God we serve.
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Paul
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Joseph and His Brothers

Summary: Exile tests faith: far from home, temple, and familiar worship, God's people had to decide whether to compromise or remain faithful. Daniel, Esther, and Mordecai show different faces of that faithfulness — quiet integrity, courageous risk, and prayerful trust. Their stories teach believers living as strangers in a foreign culture how to stand firm without losing love.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Esther Saves Her People

Summary: The faithfulness of God is His steady, covenant-keeping reliability: what He promises, He performs, even when His people fail. Israel's history is a long record of human unfaithfulness met by divine faithfulness, and the cross is its supreme proof, where God kept His ancient promise at infinite cost. Believers stake their lives on this attribute, because a faithful God can be trusted in darkness as well as in light.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Crucifixion

Summary: False teachers are an old danger: voices within the church who twist truth for influence, money, or novelty. Scripture tells believers to test every teaching against the apostles' word and to watch the teacher's life as well as their lips. The best defense against false teaching is knowing the true one deeply.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle

Summary: False teaching is doctrine that distorts the gospel, whether by denying Christ, adding works to grace, or twisting Scripture for gain. The New Testament warns about it constantly and gives tests: does it confess Jesus truly come in the flesh, does it accord with the apostles' teaching, and does it produce godliness? The response is not panic but vigilance — knowing the truth well enough to recognize counterfeits.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter; John the Apostle

Summary: Error is best refuted not by anger but by truth clearly spoken. Paul answered the Galatian agitators with the gospel itself, and the Jerusalem council settled dispute by Scripture and testimony. Refuting false teaching protects the flock and frees those being misled to return to grace.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: Family is God's first school of love, where children learn trust, obedience, and forgiveness, and where adults learn sacrifice. Scripture honors marriage and parenthood, commands children to honor parents, and warns parents not to provoke their children. The church extends family beyond blood, so that the lonely find a home and every believer has brothers and sisters in Christ.

Fear is a natural human response to danger and uncertainty, but Scripture repeatedly calls God's people not to be ruled by it because God is with them. The fear of the Lord, reverent awe, actually drives out lesser fears. Again and again, 'do not fear' comes with a promise: I am with you, I will help you, I will never leave you.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10; Psalm 56:3; Matthew 10:28-31; 2 Timothy 1:7; 1 John 4:18
RelatedDoctrines: Fear; Fear of the Lord; Trust in God
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible say about fear?; How can I stop being afraid when I cannot control the future?
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Isaiah; Matthew; 2 Timothy; 1 John

Summary: The fear of God is reverent awe before His holiness, majesty, and power — the beginning of wisdom. It is not cringing terror, for the same God who thunders at Sinai invites His people to draw near. Right fear produces obedience, humility, and freedom from every lesser fear.

To fear the Lord is to live with a constant awareness that God is holy, near, and worthy of obedience. Scripture makes it the foundation of wisdom, the motive for integrity, and the antidote to fearing people. Those who fear the Lord need fear nothing else.
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; The Ten Commandments

Summary: Fellowship is the shared life of believers with God and with one another, deeper than socializing because it is grounded in a common Lord. John writes that true fellowship with one another flows from fellowship with the Father and His Son. It shows itself in worship together, confession, generosity, and bearing one another's burdens — and it is a foretaste of the eternal communion of heaven.
RelatedQuestions: Why should I go to church?

Summary: A good start does not guarantee a good finish, and Scripture honors those who endure to the end. Paul, near death, could say he had fought the good fight and kept the faith — not because he was flawless, but because he stayed the course. Finishing well means holding fast to Christ through every season, including the last.
RelatedEvents: Paul in Rome; Paul Shipwrecked on Malta

Summary: Forgiveness is God's pardon for sin through Christ and the believer's call to release others from the debts they owe us. Scripture links receiving mercy with showing mercy, not because we earn God's favor, but because forgiven people become forgiving people. Forgiveness does not deny the hurt; it entrusts justice to God and opens the door to healing.
KeyPassages: Psalm 103:12; Matthew 6:12-15; Matthew 18:21-35; Luke 23:34; Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13; 1 John 1:9
RelatedPeople: Joseph; David; Jesus; Stephen; Peter; Paul
RelatedQuestions: How can I forgive someone who hurt me deeply?; Does forgiving mean I have to trust them again?
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Matthew; Luke; Ephesians; Colossians; Genesis
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Crucifixion; Joseph and His Brothers; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: Every life is built on something, and Scripture insists the only sure foundation is Christ. Houses built on sand collapse when storms come; those built on His word stand. The church itself rests on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, a foundation no flood can move.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Freedom in Scripture begins with liberation: Israel freed from Egypt, sinners freed from sin's power. Christ sets people free not to live for themselves but to live for God and neighbor in love. True freedom is not doing whatever we want, but being free at last to do what is right.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Passover

Summary: Jesus startled His disciples by calling them friends, not merely servants. Friendship with Christ means knowing His mind, sharing His purposes, and enjoying His presence — a relationship of love, not just duty. He proved that friendship by laying down His life for His friends.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Burning Bush

Summary: The fruit of the Spirit is the character Jesus produces in those who walk with Him: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. It cannot be manufactured by effort alone; it grows as believers abide in Christ. Where the Spirit rules, the fruit appears.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Fulfillment is what happens when God's promises land: the Law fulfilled in Christ, the prophets' hopes realized in His coming, death, and resurrection. Jesus did not discard the old story but brought it to its destination. Every promise of God finds its yes in Him.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Birth of Jesus

Summary: The cross was full payment for sin — not a deposit, not a partial settlement, but a complete satisfaction of God's justice. Hebrews stresses that Christ's one offering perfected forever those being made holy. Because the debt is fully paid, believers stand before God without condemnation and without fear.

Genealogies are more than lists of names; they are the Bible's way of saying God works through generations. They connect promise to fulfillment, Abraham to David to Jesus, and they include the unexpected — foreigners, failures, and the overlooked. In a genealogy, every name matters because every life is part of the story.

Generosity is the free, joyful sharing of what God has given, modeled on a God who gave His own Son. The Macedonian churches gave out of poverty, the widow gave out of little, and Paul taught that God loves a cheerful giver. Generosity is not measured by amount but by heart, and it loosens money's grip on the soul while meeting real needs.
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible say about money and generosity?

Summary: Glory is the weighty, radiant presence of God made visible — in creation, in the tabernacle, in Christ, and one day in the new creation. To glorify God is to honor Him as He deserves, and the chief end of humanity is to glorify God and enjoy Him forever. Every lesser glory points beyond itself to the One whose glory fills heaven and earth.

God is the one eternal, self-existent Creator of all things, infinite in power, wisdom, goodness, and love. The Bible reveals Him as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — one God in three persons — who made the world, sustains it, judges evil, and saves sinners by grace. To know God is the highest goal of human life, and every other truth finds its place in relation to Him.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:1; Exodus 3:14; Deuteronomy 6:4; Psalm 90:2; John 1:1; 1 John 4:8
RelatedQuestions: Who is God according to the Bible?
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Deuteronomy; Psalms; John; 1 John

Summary: When Israel stood trapped at the Red Sea, Moses told them to stand still and watch the Lord fight for them. Again and again Scripture shows God as warrior on behalf of His helpless people, winning battles they could never win. The Christian's confidence is the same: the battle belongs to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan

Summary: God's choice — His election — is His free, gracious decision to set His love on a people who did not earn it. Israel was chosen not for greatness but by grace, and believers are chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. Election humbles pride and anchors assurance: salvation rests on God's choice, not ours.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: God's faithfulness is the bedrock of every promise: what He says, He does, across centuries and despite human failure. From the exodus to the return from exile to the coming of Christ, His people learned that His word never returns empty. When everything else shifts, His faithfulness holds.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Wilderness Wanderings

Summary: God's glory is the radiant weight of who He is — His holiness, power, and beauty made visible. Moses glimpsed it on the mountain, Isaiah saw it fill the temple, and John saw it made flesh in Jesus. The whole creation exists to display it, and the believer's destiny is to share in it.

God's holiness is His perfect separateness from sin and His absolute moral purity, the attribute that makes angels cover their faces and sinners cry out in awe. It is not cold distance but blazing goodness, and it is why sin cannot stand in His presence apart from atonement. Believers are called to be holy as He is holy — not to earn His love, but because they belong to Him.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Isaiah; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
RelatedQuestions: What does holy mean and why does it matter?

Summary: Zephaniah dares to say God rejoices over His people with singing. This is not a distant, reluctant love but a Father's delight in His restored children. Even after exile and failure, God celebrates His people's return — a joy the prodigal's father echoes when his lost son comes home.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: God's justice means He always does what is right: defending the oppressed, judging the wicked, and keeping His world moral. It is good news for victims and a warning for oppressors, for no wrong escapes His notice forever. At the cross, justice and mercy meet: sin is judged, and sinners are saved.
RelatedEvents: Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; The Fall

Summary: Mercy is God's compassion toward those who deserve judgment — His steady refusal to give us what our sins have earned. From the golden calf to the prodigal son, Scripture shows mercy triumphing again and again. Those who receive mercy are called to show it.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Prodigal Son

Summary: God's power is His ability to do all that He wills, displayed in creation from nothing, in the exodus, and supremely in raising Jesus from the dead. No force can thwart His purposes, yet His power is exercised with wisdom and love, never as brute domination. Believers draw on that same power through the Spirit, not for self-glory but for endurance, witness, and holiness.
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Resurrection

Summary: God's presence is His nearness to His people: in the burning bush, in the tabernacle, in Christ Immanuel, and now by His Spirit. It is both comfort and challenge — the presence that guides, corrects, and never leaves. Heaven itself is described as God dwelling with His people forever.

God's promises are His word staked on His character, from Abraham's offspring to David's throne to the new covenant. They are not wishes but certainties, kept across generations and fulfilled in Christ. Believers live by trusting promises they have not yet seen fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Davidic Covenant

Summary: God's protection is His care over His people in danger, promised in images of refuge, fortress, shepherd, and wings. The Psalms are full of prayers for protection, and believers have always found God faithful — though protection does not always mean escape from harm, as the martyrs testify. Ultimate protection is eschatological: no one can snatch God's people from His hand, whatever happens in this life.

God's providence is His wise and loving governance of all things, by which He sustains creation and directs history toward His purposes. It means that nothing is random to God — not the fall of a sparrow, not the rise of empires, not the details of our lives — yet without making God the author of evil. Providence is a doctrine of comfort: the world is not in chaos, but in the hands of a Father.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Esther Saves Her People

Summary: God's provision is His faithful supply of what His people need, from manna in the wilderness to daily bread in the Lord's Prayer. Jesus taught His disciples not to be anxious about food and clothing, pointing to birds and lilies as evidence of a Father who provides. Provision does not promise wealth, but it does promise that God will not abandon His children, and it frees them to be generous with what they have.

God's sovereignty is His absolute rule over all things: He does whatever He pleases, and no purpose of His can be thwarted. Scripture holds this together with human responsibility and the reality of evil, without fully explaining the mystery. For believers, sovereignty is not a puzzle to solve but a rock to stand on, especially when life feels out of control.
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean that God is sovereign?
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: God's will has two aspects in Scripture: His sovereign decree, which always comes to pass, and His moral commands, which believers are called to obey. Discerning God's will for specific decisions involves Scripture, wisdom, counsel, and providence, not secret signs. The center of God's will is clear: that His people trust Christ, grow in holiness, and love their neighbors.

Scripture holds two truths together: God is wrathful toward evil, and He is a refuge for those who flee to Him. The flood, the Passover, and the cross all show the same pattern — judgment falls, and a shelter is provided. To take refuge in God is to be safe from the very wrath He pours out.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; The Passover

Summary: Godliness is a life shaped by God — reverent, disciplined, and good, trained by grace rather than by rules alone. Paul tells Timothy to train for it like an athlete, because it holds promise for this life and the next. True godliness is visible: it changes how we speak, spend, work, and love.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: Godly leadership is shepherding, not dominating: feeding, guiding, and protecting those entrusted to your care. Scripture warns leaders against pride and greed, and holds up Moses, Nehemiah, and above all Christ, who led by serving. The measure of a leader is the flourishing of those led.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; The Burning Bush

Summary: Good works do not save, but the saved do good works: they are the fruit of faith, prepared by God for His people to walk in. From the Good Samaritan's mercy to simple daily kindness, good works make the gospel visible. Faith without works is dead; works without faith are empty.
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Goodness is both an attribute of God — He is good in Himself and the source of every good gift — and a fruit of the Spirit in believers. God's goodness means His purposes toward His people are kind, even when His ways are hard to understand. Christians reflect that goodness by doing good to all, especially to those of the household of faith.

Creation is good because its Maker is good: light, land, sea, and creatures were declared good before humanity arrived. The psalms invite us to delight in that goodness, and Paul argues creation itself reveals God's power. Caring for creation and enjoying it are both acts of worship.

The gospel remakes relationships: enemies reconciled, masters and servants redefined as brothers, marriages and friendships reshaped by grace. Paul's letter to Philemon shows it in miniature — a runaway slave returned as a beloved brother. Where the gospel takes root, relationships change.

Gospel purity means keeping the good news unmixed: Christ plus nothing, grace without add-ons. Paul was fierce on this point, warning that a different gospel is no gospel at all. Purity protects freedom, for anything added to grace becomes a burden.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: The Gospels are the four books — Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John — that tell the story of Jesus' life, teaching, death, and resurrection. Each has its own emphasis: Matthew presents the King, Mark the Servant, Luke the Savior of all, John the divine Son. Together they give the church its founding narrative, and they are meant to be believed and obeyed, not merely admired.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Baptism of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Grace is God's unmerited favor, His kindness to people who have not earned it and cannot repay it. By grace we are saved, sustained, and shaped, from first faith to final glory. Grace humbles the proud, lifts the broken, and teaches us to extend to others what we have received.
KeyPassages: John 1:16; Romans 3:23-24; Ephesians 2:8-9; 2 Corinthians 12:9; Titus 2:11-12; Hebrews 4:16
RelatedDoctrines: Grace; Salvation by Grace; Common Grace
RelatedQuestions: What is grace and how is it different from mercy?; Can we earn God's grace?
RelatedBooks: John; Romans; Ephesians; 2 Corinthians; Hebrews; Genesis; Psalms; Titus
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Crucifixion; The Conversion of Paul; Pentecost

Summary: Gratitude is the fitting response to grace: recognizing every good gift as from God's hand and saying so. Scripture commands thanksgiving in all circumstances, not because every circumstance is good, but because God is good in every circumstance. A grateful heart is a worshiping heart.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Grief is honored in Scripture, not hurried past: psalms of lament, Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb, and the promise that God will wipe away every tear. Christian grief is real sorrow held alongside real hope — we grieve, but not as those who have no hope. God is near to the brokenhearted.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; King David; Mary of Bethany

Summary: Growth is the normal Christian life: from milk to solid food, from seed to harvest, from new birth to maturity. It comes through God's word, prayer, community, and trials, and it is measured less by speed than by direction. The call is simple: keep growing up into Christ.

Guidance is God's direction of His people's decisions, given through Scripture, the Spirit's wisdom, counsel, prayer, and providence. The Bible promises that God guides the humble, but it rarely promises a voice from heaven for every choice; more often guidance looks like wisdom applied faithfully. Believers need not fear missing God's will through one wrong turn, because God is able to redirect and redeem.
RelatedQuestions: How can I hear God's voice?

Summary: Healing is God's restoration of body, mind, and spirit, seen in Jesus' ministry and promised fully in the new creation. Christians pray for healing with confidence and humility, knowing God sometimes heals now and sometimes sustains through suffering, as with Paul's thorn. Healing ministry must be honest: it never guarantees outcomes, never blames the sick for lack of faith, and always points to the Great Physician.
KeyPassages: Exodus 15:26; Psalm 103:2-3; Isaiah 53:5; Mark 5:34; James 5:14-16; 2 Corinthians 12:7-10
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Isaiah; Mark; James; 2 Corinthians

Summary: Health is a gift to steward, not an idol to serve: Scripture treats the body as a temple of the Spirit and commends rest, work, food, and care for the sick. Illness is not necessarily punishment, and healing is not guaranteed in this life, but God cares about bodies as well as souls. Christians pursue health with gratitude and moderation, and they care for the sick as service to Christ Himself.

Heaven is God's dwelling and the believer's promised home, perfected in the new heaven and new earth where God wipes away every tear. It is not clouds and harps but a renewed creation of worship, work, reunion, and unbroken fellowship with God. The hope of heaven gives Christians courage to endure loss and live generously now.
RelatedQuestions: What will heaven be like?; Will we recognize loved ones in heaven?

Summary: Hell is the sobering reality of eternal separation from God in judgment for those who reject Him, taught plainly by Jesus Himself. It underscores both God's holiness and the urgency of the gospel, which offers rescue to everyone who turns to Christ. Christians speak of hell not with satisfaction but with tears, pleading with others to be reconciled to God.
RelatedDoctrines: Hell; Final Judgment; Wrath of God
RelatedQuestions: How can a loving God send people to hell?; Is hell eternal or temporary?

Summary: Hiddenness describes seasons when God feels absent or silent, even though He has promised never to leave His people. Job, the psalmists, and even Jesus on the cross knew this darkness, and their laments show that feeling abandoned is not the same as being abandoned. Faith in hiddenness clings to what God has already said and done, trusting His character when His hand cannot be traced.
RelatedQuestions: Why does God seem silent in my hardest seasons?

Summary: History is the arena of God's work: the Bible presents redemption not as myth but as events in time, with dates, kings, and places that can be investigated. Remembering history is a spiritual discipline in Scripture, commanded again and again so that each generation knows what God has done. Christians study history with humility, learning from both the faithfulness and the failures of those who went before.

Holiness is God's absolute purity and set-apartness, and the calling of His people to reflect His character. God declares believers holy in Christ and then commands them to pursue holiness in thought, word, and deed. Without holiness no one will see the Lord, yet it is God Himself who makes His people holy.
KeyPassages: Leviticus 19:2; Isaiah 6:3; Matthew 5:48; 2 Corinthians 7:1; Hebrews 12:14; 1 Peter 1:15-16
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Moses; Peter; Paul; Jesus; Aaron
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean that God is holy?; Why does holiness matter for ordinary Christians?
RelatedBooks: Leviticus; Isaiah; Matthew; Hebrews; 1 Peter; Exodus

Summary: Homecoming is the Bible's great arc: exiles returning, prodigals embraced, a people brought back to their God. Ezra's generation rebuilt what was ruined, and Jesus told of a Father who runs to meet a returning son. Every homecoming whispers of the final one, when God brings His people home forever.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Christian hope is confident expectation anchored in God's promises and sealed by Christ's resurrection, not mere wishful thinking. It holds fast in suffering because its anchor, Jesus, is already within the veil, interceding for His people. This hope does not disappoint, and it steadies believers to persevere with joy.
KeyPassages: Psalm 42:11; Lamentations 3:21-24; Romans 5:3-5; Romans 15:13; Hebrews 6:19; 1 Peter 1:3
RelatedQuestions: How is Christian hope different from wishful thinking?; How can I hold onto hope when life is hard?
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Lamentations; Romans; Hebrews; 1 Peter; Jeremiah
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Hope in suffering is not denial but defiance: the conviction that present pain is not the whole story. Paul argues that suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope — a hope that does not disappoint. The resurrection guarantees that suffering has an end and a purpose.

Hospitality is welcoming the stranger as Abraham welcomed travelers and as God welcomed us. It is not about impressive homes but open hearts, tables, and lives. In a world of closed doors, Christian hospitality makes the gospel visible before a word is spoken.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Hospitality must be guarded as well as generous: Scripture warns against welcoming deceivers and false teachers into the church's trust. Discernment is not the opposite of love but its protection — testing what is taught while keeping the door open to genuine need. Wise welcome loves both truth and neighbor.

Human nature is what people are by God's design and what they have become through the fall: made in God's image, yet corrupted by sin in mind, will, and affections. This dual truth explains both human greatness and human horror, and it forbids both cynicism and utopianism. Redemption does not abolish human nature but restores it, renewing the image of God in Christ.

Humanity is the race God made in His image and crowned with glory, given stewardship over creation and made for communion with Him. The fall fractured that vocation but did not erase the image, and Christ, the true man, restores what Adam lost. Every human being therefore carries a dignity no failure can remove and a destiny no eye has fully seen.

When the nation fell, God preserved a humble remnant — a small, faithful few who still trusted Him. Elijah thought he was alone; God reminded him of seven thousand who had not bowed. The remnant principle runs through Scripture: God often works through the small and the overlooked.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Humility is the honest recognition of one's place before God and others: neither self-contempt nor self-promotion, but truthful dependence. Christ is its pattern, emptying Himself to serve and die, and God promises grace to the humble while opposing the proud. Humility shows itself in listening, in admitting fault, in preferring others, and in receiving both praise and criticism without being owned by either.

Hypocrisy is the gap between profession and practice, the play-acting Jesus condemned most fiercely in religious leaders.
