It harms the church's witness because the world rightly asks whether faith changes anything. The remedy is not perfection but integrity: honest confession, accountability, and a life in which private character matches public confession.

The hypostatic union is the church's term for the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person, without confusion, change, division, or separation. Chalcedon defined it in 451 to guard the gospel: if Christ were not truly God, He could not save; if not truly man, He could not stand in our place. The doctrine is technical language for a simple wonder: God became man, and remains both forever.

Identity answers the question of who we are, and Scripture answers it first by whose we are: creatures made by God, sinners in need of grace, and, in Christ, beloved children and new creations. The world offers identities built on achievement, appearance, or affiliation, all of which shift and fail. Christian identity is received, not achieved, and it frees believers to serve without proving themselves.

Identity in Christ answers the question of who we are: new creations, children of God, members of His body, citizens of heaven. It replaces identities built on achievement, ancestry, or approval with one given by grace. To know who you are in Christ is to know what you are for.
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; The Baptism of Jesus

Summary: Idolatry is worship directed to anything other than God — statues in the ancient world, but also money, success, romance, nation, and self in every age. The prophets exposed idols as empty: they cannot see, hear, or save, and those who make them become like them. The cure is not willpower but renewed worship, loving God above all until lesser loves fall into their proper place.

The image of God is the dignity and calling stamped on every human being: to represent God, to steward creation, and to live in relationship with Him and one another. Sin has marred but not erased the image, and Christ, the perfect image, restores it in believers. This doctrine is the foundation of human rights, of the sanctity of life, and of the command to love every neighbor.
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean to be made in the image of God?

Summary: Imagination is the God-given capacity to picture what is not present — to envision, to empathize, to create, and to hope. Scripture feeds imagination with stories, visions, and parables, and the Christian imagination is trained by dwelling on what is true, noble, and lovely. Guarded well, imagination serves faith and art; left to fear and fantasy, it can mislead, which is why it needs the anchor of truth.

Inheritance is what God's children receive as His heirs: a kingdom, a new creation, and God Himself as their portion. Israel's land was a down payment; the full inheritance awaits Christ's return, incorruptible and unfading. Believers live now as heirs, already rich and not yet home.

Integrity is wholeness of character: the same person in private and public, whose yes means yes and whose life matches their words. Scripture commends the blameless walk, not as sinless perfection but as honest, consistent faithfulness. Integrity is built in small decisions over long years, and it is the quiet credential that makes a believer's witness believable.

Intelligent design is the argument that certain features of the natural world — the fine-tuning of the universe, the complexity of living things — are best explained by an intelligent cause rather than by undirected processes alone. Christians differ on how much weight this argument should bear, but most agree it fits naturally with belief in a wise Creator. Design arguments open conversations; the gospel itself is known through Christ and Scripture, not through nature alone.

Interpretation is the art and discipline of drawing meaning from a text, essential for reading the Bible well. It requires humility about our biases, attention to genre and context, and testing by the church's wisdom across time. The goal of interpretation is not to master the text for debate but to hear God and obey Him.

The gospel is an invitation, not an ultimatum: come, all who are thirsty; come to the feast; come to Me, all who labor. Isaiah, Jesus, and Revelation all sound the same open call to anyone who will hear. The church's task is to keep issuing that invitation with warmth and urgency.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Islam is the monotheistic faith founded on the Quran and the teachings of Muhammad, professing one God, Allah, and a lineage through Abraham and Ishmael. Christians and Muslims share belief in one Creator, in prophets, and in final judgment, but differ decisively on the identity of Jesus: Christians confess Him as the divine Son and crucified Savior, while Islam honors Him as a prophet and denies His divinity and crucifixion. Fair Christian engagement describes Islam accurately, loves Muslim neighbors genuinely, and presents Christ clearly without caricature or coercion.

Israel's identity was given, not earned: chosen by God, set apart as His treasured possession, and called to be a light to the nations. That identity survived slavery, wilderness, and exile because it rested on God's choice, not Israel's performance. In Christ, the church inherits that calling as God's people.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Commandments

Summary: After judgment came restoration: dry bones lived, exiles returned, and the temple rose again. Restoration was never merely political; it was God renewing His covenant and His people from within. The prophets' vision points beyond return from Babylon to the new covenant and the new creation.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Jesus Christ is the central figure of the Christian faith: the eternal Son of God who became man, lived sinlessly, died on the cross for sinners, and rose again on the third day. His name joins His humanity (Jesus) with His office (Christ, the anointed King), and the Gospels present Him as the fulfillment of Israel's hopes and the Savior of the world. To know Jesus is, for Christians, to know God Himself.
RelatedQuestions: Who is Jesus Christ?; Why did Jesus have to die on the cross?; Did Jesus really rise from the dead?
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Baptism of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Joy in Scripture is deeper than happiness, rooted in who God is and what He has done, so it can endure even in sorrow and suffering. The Psalms sing it, Jesus promised His joy to His disciples, and joy is a fruit of the Spirit in every believer. The joy of the Lord is our strength.
KeyPassages: Nehemiah 8:10; Psalm 16:11; Habakkuk 3:17-18; John 15:11; Philippians 4:4; Galatians 5:22
RelatedBooks: Nehemiah; Psalms; Habakkuk; John; Philippians; Galatians
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; The Birth of Jesus; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Joy in hardship sounds impossible until you see Paul singing in prison or Habakkuk rejoicing with no harvest in sight. Christian joy does not depend on circumstances but on Christ, who is present in them. It is a stubborn gladness that suffering cannot cancel.
RelatedEvents: Paul Shipwrecked on Malta; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: Judgment is God's righteous verdict on human deeds, promised throughout Scripture and culminating in the final judgment when Christ returns. It is sobering because God sees all and judges justly, yet it is also good news: evil will not have the last word, and wrongs will be set right. For believers, judgment is faced with confidence, not terror, because Christ has borne their condemnation.
RelatedQuestions: How can a loving God send people to hell?; What does the Bible say about hell?
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Judgment and mercy meet in God's character: He judges sin truly and forgives sinners freely. The psalmist says mercy and truth meet together, and James warns that mercy triumphs over judgment for the merciful. At the cross both are fully satisfied — sin condemned, sinners welcomed.
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

Summary: False teachers face a severe judgment, Scripture warns, because they lead others astray while claiming God's name. Peter and Jude describe their end soberly, not gleefully — as a warning to the church to guard the truth. The severity of the judgment matches the seriousness of the trust betrayed.
RelatedPeople: Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Jesus

Summary: Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, but a century later Nahum announced its fall: a city that returned to violence would face God's judgment. Nineveh's story warns that repentance must be real and lasting, and that no empire, however great, stands outside God's justice.

Pride invites judgment because it claims God's place: Babel's tower, Nebuchadnezzar's boast, and every heart that exalts itself. God humbles the proud not out of cruelty but to restore truth — that He alone is great. The humbled, by contrast, are lifted up.

Justice is God's righteous character in action: He always does what is right, defends the vulnerable, and will judge evil fairly. Scripture calls God's people to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly, reflecting their just King in a broken world. At the cross, God's justice and mercy meet, as sin is punished and sinners are pardoned.
KeyPassages: Genesis 18:25; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 89:14; Micah 6:8; Amos 5:24; Romans 3:25-26
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Amos; Micah; Jesus; Paul; Moses
RelatedQuestions: How can a loving God also be just?; What does the Bible say about doing justice today?
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Deuteronomy; Psalms; Micah; Amos; Romans; Isaiah

Summary: Justification is God's gracious act of declaring sinners righteous in His sight through faith in Christ alone. It is a legal verdict, not a process: the moment a person trusts Jesus, Christ's righteousness is credited to them. Justified believers have peace with God and no condemnation to fear.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:6; Romans 3:28; Romans 4:5; Romans 5:1; Romans 8:1; Galatians 2:16; Philippians 3:9
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean to be justified by faith?; How can God declare sinners righteous and still be just?

Summary: Justification by faith is the heart of the gospel: sinners are declared righteous before God not by works but by trusting Christ. Abraham believed and it was credited to him as righteousness, and the same faith credits righteousness to all who believe. Justification is a gift received, never a wage earned.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Crucifixion

Summary: Karma is the belief, common in Hinduism and Buddhism, that actions carry moral consequences across lifetimes, shaping future rebirth. Christians recognize the biblical truth that actions have consequences — we reap what we sow — but reject the impersonal cycle of rebirth: Scripture teaches one life, one death, and one judgment, with salvation by grace rather than by accumulated merit. The gospel answers karma's burden with a Savior who bears what we cannot repay.

Kindness is love in action toward others, gentle, generous, and undeserved — a fruit of the Spirit and a mark of God's own character. Scripture commends small kindnesses as well as great ones: a cup of water, a word of encouragement, a welcome to the stranger. Kindness is not weakness; it is strength under control, choosing to bless even when retaliation would be easier.
KeyPassages: Ruth 2:8-13; Proverbs 11:17; Luke 6:35-36; Galatians 5:22; Ephesians 4:32; Titus 3:4-5
RelatedBooks: Ruth; Proverbs; Luke; Galatians; Ephesians; Titus

Summary: Kingdom living is life under God's reign here and now: seeking His kingdom first, practicing its values of mercy, purity, and peacemaking. It is not waiting for heaven but inhabiting heaven's rule on earth, in homes, workplaces, and neighborhoods. The Sermon on the Mount is its charter.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; Pentecost

Summary: The kingdom of God is God's reign breaking into the world through Jesus, already present wherever Christ is obeyed and not yet complete until He returns. Jesus announced it, taught it in parables, and demonstrated it in healings and deliverance. Believers enter it by new birth and live now as citizens of a kingdom that will never end.
KeyPassages: Daniel 2:44; Mark 1:14-15; Matthew 6:10; Matthew 6:33; Luke 17:20-21; John 3:3-5; Revelation 11:15
RelatedPeople: Daniel; Jesus; John the Baptist; Nicodemus; Paul
RelatedDoctrines: Kingdom of God; Eschatology; Lordship of Christ
RelatedQuestions: What is the kingdom of God?; Is the kingdom of God already here or still coming?
RelatedBooks: Daniel; Matthew; Mark; Luke; John; Revelation
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Matthew's phrase 'kingdom of heaven' describes God's reign breaking into the world through Jesus. It arrives quietly — like seed, yeast, and treasure — yet it overturns every other allegiance. To enter it is to submit to the King and receive a citizenship that outlasts every earthly kingdom.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Scripture contrasts the kingdoms of this world — built on power, wealth, and pride — with the kingdom of God, which lasts forever. Empires rise and fall, from Babel to Rome, but Daniel saw a kingdom that would never be destroyed. Believers live as citizens of the lasting kingdom while sojourning in temporary ones.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Daniel in the Lions' Den

Summary: Kingship belongs to God: the psalms call Him King over all the earth, and Israel's kings were meant to rule as His deputies. Human kingship failed again and again, which is why the promise of a perfect King mattered so much. All authority is borrowed; only God's kingship is absolute.

Christ's kingship was proclaimed at His birth, mocked at His trial, and vindicated at His resurrection. He reigns now from heaven, and He will return to reign openly, every knee bowing before Him. To confess Jesus as Lord is to pledge allegiance to the true King.

Knowledge of Christ is not mere information about Him but a living acquaintance that transforms. Paul counted everything loss beside knowing Christ, and Peter urges believers to grow in that knowledge. To know Him is eternal life, and it deepens through Scripture, prayer, and obedience.

Knowledge of God is more than information about Him; it is personal acquaintance through His word, His works, and His Son. Scripture says eternal life itself is knowing God and Jesus Christ, and it warns that knowledge without love puffs up. True knowledge of God transforms: it humbles the proud, comforts the fearful, and sends believers out in obedience.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Hosea; Jesus; Paul; Simon Peter

Summary: The Lamb is one of Scripture's richest pictures of Christ: the Passover lamb whose blood sheltered Israel, the lamb provided on Mount Moriah, and Isaiah's suffering servant led like a lamb to the slaughter. John the Baptist announced Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Revelation crowns the Lamb who was slain as worthy of all worship.
KeyPassages: Genesis 22:7-8; Exodus 12:3-13; Isaiah 53:7; John 1:29; 1 Peter 1:18-19; Revelation 5:12
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Exodus; Isaiah; John; 1 Peter; Revelation
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Moses; Isaiah; Jesus; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Passover; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Lament is the honest prayer of grief, complaint, and longing directed to God, modeled in a third of the Psalms and in the cries of Job and Jeremiah. It refuses both denial and despair: it names pain plainly while still addressing God as Lord and ending, often, in trust. The church needs lament because faith that cannot grieve cannot fully hope.

Language is a gift that builds and breaks: it confused Babel, united Pentecost, and daily shapes communities. Scripture warns that the tongue is a small fire with great power, and calls believers to speak truth with grace. How we use words reveals what rules our hearts.

Biblical leadership is shepherding, not lording: leading by serving, character, and example as Jesus did when He washed His disciples' feet. God raises leaders to equip His people, guard the truth, and care for the flock at cost to themselves. The measure of a leader is not platform or power but faithfulness and love for people.
KeyPassages: Joshua 1:8-9; Proverbs 11:14; Mark 10:42-45; John 13:14-15; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:7-9; 1 Peter 5:2-3
RelatedPeople: Moses; Joshua; David; Nehemiah; Jesus; Paul; Timothy
RelatedQuestions: What makes a good leader according to the Bible?; How should Christians respond to flawed leaders?

Summary: Life in Scripture is God's gift, breathed into dust, and it means more than mere existence: it is fellowship with the living God. Sin brought death into the world, but Christ came that His people might have life abundantly, now and forever. The Christian hope is not escape from embodied life but its redemption — resurrection life in a renewed creation.

Light in Scripture stands for God's truth, purity, guidance, and life, shining first at creation and finally in the face of Christ. Jesus, the Light of the World, exposes darkness, guides our steps, and calls His people the light of the world. Walking in the light means honest, joyful fellowship with God and one another.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:3; Psalm 119:105; Isaiah 60:1; Matthew 5:14-16; John 8:12; 1 John 1:5-7
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Isaiah; Matthew; John; 1 John
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Birth of Jesus; Transfiguration

Summary: Scripture opens with God speaking light into darkness, and that contrast runs through the whole Bible as a picture of good and evil, truth and falsehood, life and death. Jesus declared Himself the Light of the World, and His followers are called to shine as lights in a dark world. In the new creation, darkness will be gone forever.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:3-4; Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 9:2; John 1:5; John 8:12; Ephesians 5:8; Revelation 22:5
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Psalms; Isaiah; John; Ephesians; Revelation
RelatedEvents: Creation; The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection
Places: Garden of Eden; Bethlehem; Golgotha; Jerusalem

Summary: Listening well is the neglected half of love: giving full attention to another person without planning a reply, correcting, or turning the conversation to oneself. James urges believers to be quick to listen and slow to speak, and Jesus modeled listening that dignified the overlooked. Good listening is a form of hospitality, making room for another's story before offering answers.

Living faith is faith with hands and feet: trusting God and acting on that trust, as Abraham did when he left home and Rahab did when she hid the spies. James insists that faith without works is dead — not because works save, but because real trust always moves. Living faith obeys, gives, forgives, and goes.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Walls of Jericho

Summary: Living hope is hope made alive by Christ's resurrection — not wishful thinking but confident expectation of an inheritance kept in heaven. Peter writes to suffering believers that this hope guards them through trials and purifies them for glory. It is called living because it grows, endures, and changes how we live today.

Logic is the disciplined study of sound reasoning: identifying valid arguments, exposing fallacies, and following evidence where it leads. Scripture commends reasoned persuasion — Isaiah invites Israel to reason together, and Paul argued daily in synagogues and marketplaces. Logic cannot by itself produce faith, but it serves faith by clarifying claims, testing arguments, and helping believers think clearly about God and His world.

Longing is the ache for what is missing — for home, for wholeness, for God — that runs through human experience and through Scripture. Augustine said our hearts are restless until they rest in God, and the Psalms turn longing into prayer. Christian hope does not deny longing but directs it: every good longing is a signpost toward the God who will one day satisfy it fully.
RelatedPeople: King David; Paul; John the Apostle

Summary: Lordship is the confession that Jesus is Lord — that He has the right to command every area of life, not only its religious corners. The earliest Christian creed was simply Jesus is Lord, a claim that relativized every other loyalty, including Caesar's. Lordship is good news before it is a demand: the One who rules is the crucified and risen Savior who lays down His life for His people.

Love is the defining mark of God Himself and the greatest commandment for His people: to love God fully and love neighbors as ourselves. At the cross we see love's true measure, not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son. The Spirit pours God's love into believers' hearts so they can love sacrificially, truthfully, and without fear.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37-39; John 3:16; John 15:13; Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13; 1 John 4:7-19
RelatedDoctrines: Love of God; Agape; Greatest Commandment
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible mean by love?; How can I love difficult people?
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Matthew; John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; 1 John; Psalms
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Crucifixion; The Last Supper; Creation

Summary: Love for God is the first and greatest commandment: to love Him with all heart, soul, mind, and strength. It is not sentiment alone but loyalty shown in obedience, worship, and trust. We love because He first loved us, and that love spills over to every neighbor.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount; The Last Supper

Summary: The love of God is His steadfast, self-giving commitment to His people, shown most clearly in sending His Son while we were still sinners. It is not sentimental indulgence: God's love disciplines, judges evil, and refuses to abandon. Believers live from this love, not for it — secure enough to love others because they are already loved.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Jesus; Paul; John the Apostle

Summary: Loyalty is steadfast faithfulness to God and to others through changing circumstances, the quality Ruth showed Naomi and Jonathan showed David. It is tested most when loyalty costs something — when a friend fails, a cause falters, or obedience is inconvenient. Christian loyalty is ultimately loyalty to Christ, which orders every lesser loyalty and never asks believers to be loyal to wrongdoing.

God's majesty is his royal splendor: the weight of glory that makes mountains tremble and angels cover their faces. Scripture clothes him in light, seats him above the flood, and crowns him with honor no creature can rival. To behold his majesty is both to tremble and to trust, for the majestic God is also the shepherd who carries his lambs close to his heart.

Manipulation is influence that bypasses honesty and consent, steering people toward a choice they would not freely make. Scripture contrasts it with persuasion that tells the truth and respects the other person's freedom: Paul insists he did not use flattery or hidden motives, and Jesus never coerced belief. Christians are called to spot manipulation - in leaders, in marketing, in relationships, even in their own hearts - and to replace it with plain speech, fair dealing, and respect for conscience.

The Bible we read rests on thousands of handwritten copies made over centuries, and the study of those manuscripts is how scholars recover the original text. Copyists made mistakes, but the sheer number and spread of manuscripts let us compare readings and spot errors with unusual confidence. For Christians, manuscript evidence is not a threat to faith but a reason for it: no doctrine hangs on a disputed reading, and the text's transmission is remarkably well documented.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: Marriage is God's good design from creation: a lifelong covenant between a man and a woman picturing Christ's faithful love for His church. It calls husbands and wives to sacrificial love, forgiveness, and partnership in God's purposes. Strong marriages are built not on feelings alone but on covenant commitment renewed daily in grace.
KeyPassages: Genesis 2:24; Proverbs 18:22; Malachi 2:14; Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:25-33; 1 Peter 3:7
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible say about marriage?; How can a Christian marriage survive hard seasons?

Summary: Marriage in Scripture is a covenant, not merely a contract: a solemn, lifelong bond in which husband and wife become one flesh and mirror God's faithful love for his people. Genesis gives its pattern, the prophets use it to picture God's covenant with Israel, and Paul lifts it higher still as a picture of Christ and the church. Guarding marriage therefore guards a living sermon about God's keeping love.

Martyrdom is witness sealed with death: believers who would rather die than deny Christ. The word itself means witness, and the New Testament treats martyrs not as victims of a failed cause but as conquerors whose blood, Tertullian said, is the seed of the church. From Stephen to the persecuted church today, martyrdom raises hard questions about courage, God's protection, and why faithfulness sometimes costs everything.

Life's meaning is the question Ecclesiastes presses hardest: what lasts, what satisfies, what makes the brief years under the sun worth living? Apart from God, even wisdom, wealth, and work turn to vapor; with him, ordinary days gain weight and purpose. Scripture's answer is not a technique but a Person: we are made by God, for God, and find our meaning in fearing him, keeping his commandments, and enjoying his gifts as from his hand.

Mercy is God's compassion toward the miserable and guilty, withholding the judgment we deserve and moving to relieve our distress. From Exodus to the Gospels, God delights in mercy and calls His people blessed when they show it to others. Every believer lives daily on mercy, receiving fresh compassion each morning.
KeyPassages: Exodus 34:6-7; Psalm 103:8-13; Lamentations 3:22-23; Micah 7:18; Matthew 5:7; Luke 6:36; Titus 3:5; James 2:13
RelatedPeople: Moses; David; Hosea; Jesus; Paul; Jonah
RelatedQuestions: What is the difference between mercy and grace?; How can I show mercy without excusing sin?
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Lamentations; Micah; Matthew; Titus; Luke; Ephesians
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Good Samaritan; The Exodus and the Red Sea; Jonah and Nineveh; The Crucifixion

Summary: Messiah means anointed one, the promised king, priest, and prophet God would send to rescue His people. Israel waited centuries for this figure, and Christians confess that Jesus of Nazareth is He: anointed at His baptism, crucified as the suffering servant, and raised as the reigning Lord. Understanding the Messiah means reading the Old Testament's promises and the Gospels' claims together, since Jesus deliberately fulfilled some expectations and overturned others.
KeyPassages: Psalms 2:1-12; Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 53:1-12; Daniel 9:24-27; Luke 4:16-21; John 1:41
RelatedQuestions: Which prophecies did Jesus fulfill?
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Baptism of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Israel waited for a Messiah: an anointed king from David's line who would defeat God's enemies and reign in righteousness. Jesus is that King, though his crown came by a cross and his throne by resurrection. He reigns now over all things for the good of his church, and one day every knee will bow to him.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Long before Jesus came, God's people lived on promises: a seed who would crush the serpent, a son of David whose kingdom would never end, a suffering servant who would bear our griefs. That hope sustained exiles, prophets, and ordinary families through centuries of waiting. In Jesus the hope arrived, and because he rose, our hope now looks forward to his return and the renewal of all things.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Resurrection

Summary: Long before Jesus was born, Israel's prophets spoke of a coming deliverer: born in Bethlehem, from David's line, a servant who would suffer for His people and a king who would reign forever. Christians point to dozens of such prophecies fulfilled in Jesus' birth, ministry, death, and resurrection as evidence that His coming was planned, not improvised. These prophecies also discipline how we read them: not as a code to crack, but as promises that find their yes in Christ.
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:15; Micah 5:2; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 53:1-12; Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 1:22-23
RelatedQuestions: Which prophecies did Jesus fulfill?

Summary: Methodism is the movement born from John Wesley's preaching in eighteenth-century England, shaped by disciplined methods of prayer, study, and small-group accountability. Its emphases - grace available to all, holiness of heart and life, and faith working through love - spread through revival preaching and the circuit riders who carried the gospel across frontiers. Methodism reminds the church that structure can serve passion, and that personal holiness and social compassion belong together.

Ministry is service done in Christ's name, and the New Testament insists it belongs to the whole church, not only to professionals. Pastors equip, but every believer is gifted to build up the body: teaching, serving, giving, encouraging, and showing mercy. Healthy ministry flows from character before platform, from a life with God before work for God, and it is measured less by visibility than by faithfulness to the people entrusted to us.

Miracles are God's acts that break the ordinary pattern of nature to reveal His power and purposes. In Scripture they cluster around decisive moments - the exodus, the ministries of Elijah and Elisha, Jesus, and the apostles - and they function as signs, not spectacles: the feeding of thousands points to the Bread of Life, and healings announce the kingdom breaking in. Christians disagree about whether miraculous gifts continue today in the same way, but agree that God remains free to act and that every miracle points beyond itself to Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Plagues; Elijah on Mount Carmel; The Feeding of the Five Thousand; Raising of Lazarus

Summary: Mission is the church's calling to carry the good news to people who have not yet heard it, near and far. It flows from God's own mission: the Father sends the Son, and the Son sends His people, empowered by the Spirit. Mission takes many forms - evangelism, church planting, mercy work, translation - but its center never moves: proclaiming Jesus Christ, in word and deed, so that people from every nation can know Him.
RelatedQuestions: What exactly is the gospel I should share?

Summary: Missions is the organized work of taking the gospel across cultures and languages, from the apostle Paul's journeys to today's missionaries and translators. It has always involved more than preaching: learning languages, respecting cultures, planting churches, and serving communities. The history of missions includes both remarkable sacrifice and real failures, and modern missions tries to learn from both - partnering with local believers rather than replacing them.
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: Money is a tool, a test, and a temptation: Scripture speaks about it more than almost any other everyday subject. Jesus warned that wealth can quietly become a master, while also commending generous, cheerful giving and honest work. The Bible's money wisdom is practical - avoid debt, provide for family, be content, hold wealth loosely - and its center is trust: everything we have is received, and generosity is how we say we believe it.

Monotheism is belief in one God, and it sets the Bible apart in the ancient world, where every nation had its pantheon. Israel's confession - the LORD our God, the LORD is one - was both theology and loyalty: one God means one allegiance, one Creator, one Judge, one Savior. Christianity holds this confession together with the Trinity: one God in three persons, not three gods, a mystery the church has carefully guarded ever since.

Moral responsibility is the truth that people are answerable for their choices: we are not merely products of our circumstances, and our actions genuinely matter. Scripture holds this together with grace - we are responsible, yet unable to save ourselves - and with God's sovereignty, without letting either cancel the other. It shapes how Christians think about guilt, repentance, justice, and parenting: we can and must choose, and our choices form who we become.

Morality asks what is right and wrong, and the Bible grounds the answer in God's character rather than in majority opinion or personal feeling. The moral law - love God, love neighbor, summarized in the Ten Commandments and the Sermon on the Mount - describes the life God designed for human flourishing. Christians confess we do not live it perfectly, which is why morality in Scripture always walks hand in hand with mercy: the law shows us our need, and grace meets it.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Myths are traditional stories that explain the world, and the Bible's relationship to them is more interesting than simple rejection. Some biblical stories share shapes with ancient myths - floods, heroes, creation battles - but retell them with a decisive difference: one Creator, a good creation, and a God who acts in real history. Christians also ask whether myths can carry truth: C. S. Lewis called the gospel a myth become fact, a story with myth's power that actually happened.

Nations in Scripture are more than political units: God made the peoples, scattered them, judges them, and promises to gather them. The Old Testament moves between God's particular love for Israel and His universal purpose for all nations, and Revelation ends with people from every tribe and tongue worshiping together. For Christians, this relativizes every national loyalty: our deepest citizenship is in heaven, and no nation is the kingdom of God.

Nature is God's first book, displaying His power and care to everyone, everywhere. Scripture treats creation as good, ordered, and purposeful - not divine itself, and not an accident - and calls humans its stewards, not its owners. Nature also witnesses against us: its beauty points to a Creator, and its brokenness groans under the same curse that afflicts us, waiting for the renewal promised in Christ.

God is not far off: he draws near to the brokenhearted, dwells with the humble, and invites his people to draw near in return. The tabernacle, the temple, and finally the incarnation all tell one story: God closing the distance sin created. James promises simply that if we draw near to God, he will draw near to us, and Psalm 73 confesses that the nearness of God is our good.

After the judges' cycles of failure, Israel cried out for a king, and God gave them first Saul, then David, teaching them that no human king could finally save. The longing itself was right: God's people need a righteous ruler to lead them in God's ways and defend them from their enemies. That need is answered only in Jesus, the King whose reign brings justice without tyranny and victory without violence.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; King Saul; King David; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Anointing of Saul as King; David Becomes King

Summary: A neighbor, Jesus taught, is not a category of person but anyone in need whom we have the power to help - including the stranger and the enemy. The parable of the Good Samaritan redefines neighborliness from proximity to mercy: seeing, stopping, and spending yourself for someone else's good. Loving neighbor is how love for God becomes visible, and Scripture insists it includes the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the outsider.
RelatedQuestions: How can I love difficult people?

Summary: God promised through Jeremiah a covenant written on hearts, not stone, with sins forgiven and God known personally. Jesus inaugurated it at the Last Supper, saying the cup is the new covenant in his blood. We live under it now: forgiven, indwelt by the Spirit, and called to a new life of obedience from the inside out.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Crucifixion; Pentecost

Summary: The Bible ends where it began, only greater: a new heavens and new earth where God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear. That future has already broken in, for anyone in Christ is a new creation, raised to new life by the Spirit. New creation hope steadies us now and shapes how we care for God's world and one another.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:31; Isaiah 65:17; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15; Revelation 21:1-5; Romans 8:19-21
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Isaiah; 2 Corinthians; Galatians; Revelation; Romans

Summary: God promised through Ezekiel to remove hearts of stone and give hearts of flesh, writing his law within and putting his Spirit in his people. A new heart is not self-improvement but resurrection: God replaces rebellion with responsiveness, so that we love what he loves and turn from what we once loved. This is the inward miracle behind every true conversion and every lasting change.

New life is the fresh start God gives through faith in Christ: the old self buried, a new self raised. The New Testament describes it with several pictures - new birth, new creation, resurrection - all pointing to the same reality: forgiveness of sins and the Spirit's power to live differently. New life begins in a moment but grows over a lifetime, as believers learn to walk in step with the Spirit and put off the old patterns of sin.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Resurrection

Summary: The Nicene Creed is the church's ancient summary of the faith, forged at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 to defend the full deity of Christ against Arianism. In a few hundred words it confesses one God, Jesus Christ as true God and true man, and the Holy Spirit as Lord and giver of life. Christians across traditions still recite it as a boundary of orthodoxy and a shared confession that predates every modern denomination.

Obedience is doing what God asks because we trust the One who asks it. Scripture never treats it as a cold duty: in Deuteronomy it flows from remembering deliverance, in the Psalms from delight in God's law, and in John's Gospel from love for Jesus. Obedience is also where faith becomes visible - Abraham leaving home, Mary saying let it be, Jesus in Gethsemane - and where blessing, discipline, and formation all meet.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:4-9; 1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 119:1-8; Luke 1:38; John 14:15; Hebrews 5:8-9
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; 1 Samuel; Psalms; Luke; John; Hebrews

Summary: The occult covers practices that seek hidden knowledge or power apart from God: divination, spiritism, magic, and astrology. Scripture forbids them consistently, not because they are harmless superstition but because they open doors to spiritual realities God has not given us to traffic in. The Christian answer is not fascination or fear but trust: God's Word and Spirit give all the guidance we need, and Christ's authority is greater than any power the occult claims.

The Old Testament is the first three-quarters of the Christian Bible: law, history, poetry, and prophecy spanning from creation to the return from exile. Christians read it as God's own story, not as background material - the promises, patterns, and problems that the New Testament claims Jesus fulfills. Reading it well means honoring its genres, its ancient context, and its central arc: a holy God pursuing a wandering people.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Faithfulness in Scripture almost always meets opposition: Nehemiah's wall-builders held a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other, Daniel's enemies plotted against his prayers, and the apostles were ordered to stop speaking in Jesus' name. Opposition is not a sign that God has abandoned his work; often it is the sign that the work matters. God's people answer it with prayer, courage, and steady obedience, trusting the Lord who builds what no enemy can tear down.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Martyrdom of Stephen

Summary: Original sin is the doctrine that Adam's first sin in Eden affected all humanity, so every person is born with a fallen nature inclined away from God. It explains why sin is universal and why we need a Savior rather than just a better example. In Christ, the second Adam, God provides the righteousness Adam lost.
RelatedQuestions: Is original sin unjust?; Are we guilty for Adam's sin?

Summary: Origins asks where everything came from: the universe, life, and humanity itself. The Bible answers with a Creator who made all things good and purposeful, while Christians differ on how Genesis relates to scientific accounts of deep time and evolution. What unites orthodox Christians is the core confession: the universe is not an accident, human beings bear God's image, and creation's order reflects a rational Creator - convictions that made modern science itself possible.
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?

Summary: At Pentecost the promised Spirit fell like wind and fire, filling ordinary disciples with boldness to speak of Jesus in every tongue. The outpouring Joel foresaw had come: sons and daughters prophesying, old men dreaming dreams, God's presence poured out on all flesh. The same Spirit still fills the church today, giving gifts for service and power for witness until Christ returns.

Parenting is the God-given calling to raise children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, teaching them God's words in everyday life. It balances firm guidance with tenderness, aiming not just at good behavior but at hearts that know and love God. Parents depend on the same grace they preach, pointing their children to a perfect Father.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:4-7; Psalm 127:3; Proverbs 22:6; Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21; 2 Timothy 3:15
RelatedQuestions: What does the Bible say about raising children?; How do I teach my children about God at home?

Summary: God's work has always been shared work: Paul and Barnabas, Priscilla and Aquila, Paul and Timothy, partners in the gospel bound by affection, trust, and a common mission. Partnership is more than efficiency; it is the shape of the body of Christ, where gifts differ and burdens are carried together. Even the strongest leaders in Scripture leaned on companions, reminding us that ministry done alone is ministry done wrong.

Patience reflects God's own character, for He is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love toward a rebellious world. Abraham waited for a son, Joseph waited in prison, and God's people waited centuries for the Messiah, learning that God's timing is never wasted. The Spirit grows patience in us as we wait hopefully for Christ's return.
KeyPassages: Exodus 34:6; Psalm 40:1; Romans 8:25; Galatians 5:22; James 5:7-8; 2 Peter 3:9
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Romans; Galatians; James; 2 Peter
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; Joseph and His Brothers; The Birth of Jesus

Summary: Peace — shalom — is wholeness with God, with others, and within ourselves, lost in the Fall and restored through Christ who is our peace. Jesus gives a peace the world cannot give, guarding hearts and minds even in trouble. One day the Prince of Peace will reign, and swords will become ploughshares.
KeyPassages: Numbers 6:24-26; Isaiah 9:6; John 14:27; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14; Philippians 4:7
RelatedBooks: Numbers; Isaiah; John; Romans; Ephesians; Philippians
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Persecution is hostility faced for following Christ, from mockery and exclusion to imprisonment and death. Jesus promised it plainly and called it blessed, and the New Testament treats it as normal for a church that lives differently from the world around it. Christians respond not with retaliation but with endurance, prayer for enemies, and solidarity with suffering brothers and sisters - and by counting the cost honestly before promising the world that faith is easy.

Perseverance is the steady continuance of faith through trials, doubts, and long obedience - and, in Reformed theology, the conviction that God preserves His people to the end. Scripture holds both sides: believers must endure, and God is the one who keeps them enduring. The warnings against falling away and the promises that nothing can separate us from God's love are not contradictions but partners, urging vigilance without despair.
KeyPassages: John 10:27-29; Romans 8:28-39; Philippians 1:6; Hebrews 10:35-39; James 1:2-4; Revelation 2:10
RelatedQuestions: Can a Christian be sanctified and still struggle with sin?
RelatedBooks: John; Romans; Philippians; Hebrews; James; Revelation

Summary: Philosophy is the love of wisdom: asking the big questions about truth, goodness, beauty, and existence with reasoned argument. Scripture engages philosophy rather than ignoring it - Paul debated Stoics and Epicureans in Athens, and the church has used philosophical tools to clarify doctrines like the Trinity ever since. The Christian posture is discerning: all truth is God's truth, but human wisdom must bow to revelation where the two conflict, and reason serves faith rather than ruling it.

Pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, undertaken to seek God, remember His acts, or mark a turning point. Israel's feasts drew pilgrims to Jerusalem three times a year, and Christians have walked to sites of biblical memory ever since - while remembering that the destination is a person, not a place. The Christian life itself is often described as pilgrimage: strangers and exiles traveling toward a heavenly country, learning dependence one step at a time.

A plea is prayer at its most honest: an urgent cry for mercy, help, or deliverance when we have nothing left to offer. The psalms are full of pleas: How long, O Lord? And Jesus honored the blind beggar's plea, Son of David, have mercy on me. God does not despise a pleading heart; he bends his ear to it, and often the plea itself is the beginning of faith.

Praise is God's people answering his goodness with song, speech, and shouting joy. The Psalms model it in every season: praise rises from deliverance, from creation's beauty, and even from the depths. Praise is both a gift we offer and a weapon against despair, because it fixes our eyes on who God is rather than on what we fear.

Prayer is speaking with God as His children, bringing Him praise, confession, thanks, and requests in Jesus' name. God invites His people to pray persistently and honestly, promising to hear and answer according to His wisdom and love. Prayer does not change God's character, but it changes us and is a means God uses to accomplish His purposes.
KeyPassages: Psalm 145:18; Matthew 6:9-13; Luke 18:1; Romans 8:26; Philippians 4:6-7; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16
RelatedPeople: Hannah; Daniel; Jesus; Paul; Elijah; Abraham
RelatedQuestions: Does prayer change God's mind?; Why does God seem not to answer some prayers?
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Matthew; Luke; Philippians; James; Genesis; 1 Samuel; Daniel; Hebrews
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Daniel in the Lions' Den; The Crucifixion; Pentecost

Summary: Preaching is the public proclamation of God's Word, calling hearers to believe and obey. From the prophets to the apostles to the church today, preaching has carried a double weight: faithfully explaining the text and urgently applying it to real lives. Good preaching is not performance but stewardship - the preacher stands under the Word before standing before the people, and the goal is never admiration but transformation.

The presence of God is His nearness to His people - in the tabernacle's cloud, in the temple, in Jesus' incarnation, and now in the Spirit dwelling within believers. Scripture holds together God's everywhere-presence with His special, covenant presence: He is never absent, yet He draws near in worship, in suffering, and in obedience. The Christian hope is presence made permanent: one day we will see Him face to face, and the ache of distance will end.
KeyPassages: Exodus 33:14-16; Psalm 16:11; Psalm 139:7-12; Matthew 28:20; John 14:16-17; Revelation 21:1-4
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; The Ten Commandments; Pentecost

Summary: God's preservation is his keeping power: he guarded Noah through the flood, kept a remnant in exile, and preserves his people to the end. Jude calls believers kept for Jesus Christ, and Jesus promised that no one can snatch his sheep from his hand. Preservation is not immunity from hardship but security through it: God keeps what is his, and he will finish what he began.

Pride is the inflated sense of self that puts us at the center where God belongs - the root sin behind the fall and the quiet engine of most others. Scripture warns that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, and it prescribes the cures: remembering we are creatures, receiving everything as gift, and serving others. Humility is not thinking less of ourselves but thinking of ourselves less, because our eyes are fixed on Christ.
KeyPassages: Proverbs 16:18; Isaiah 14:12-15; Daniel 4:28-37; Luke 18:9-14; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5-6
RelatedBooks: Proverbs; Isaiah; Daniel; Luke; James; 1 Peter

Summary: In the Old Testament, priests stood between God and his people, offering sacrifices and blessing in God's name; Aaron and his sons carried this holy, costly calling. The New Testament announces a better priesthood: Jesus, our great high priest, offered himself once for all, and now all believers are a royal priesthood with direct access to God. We no longer need a human mediator, because the Mediator lives forever to intercede for us.

Life is short and demands are endless, so Scripture urges us to choose what matters first: God's kingdom, his people, and the work he has actually given us. Martha learned that one thing is necessary; Mary chose the good portion at Jesus' feet. Right priorities are not found by doing more but by seeking first what God seeks, and letting the rest find its place beneath it.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Martha; Mary of Bethany; Paul

Summary: A promise is a word you can build a life on, and the Bible is held together by God's promises: to Abraham, to David, to Israel, and finally to all who trust in Christ. Unlike human promises, God's cannot fail, because they rest on His character rather than on circumstances. The Christian life is learning to live between promise and fulfillment - trusting what God has said while waiting for what He has not yet done.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Davidic Covenant

Summary: The promises of God are His sworn commitments scattered through Scripture - hundreds of them, covering provision, presence, forgiveness, guidance, and eternal life. Christians read them as a family inheritance: every promise finds its yes in Christ, and each one invites trust in a specific situation. The discipline is to claim promises as God gave them, without twisting them into guarantees He never made or ignoring the conditions He attached.
KeyPassages: Genesis 28:15; Deuteronomy 31:6; Isaiah 41:10; Matthew 28:20; Romans 8:28; Hebrews 13:5-6
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Deuteronomy; Isaiah; Matthew; Romans; Hebrews
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; Davidic Covenant

Summary: Prophecy is God's word spoken through His chosen messengers to warn, comfort, and reveal His plans, including promises fulfilled in Jesus. True prophecy always agrees with God's character and often calls His people back to covenant faithfulness. Studying prophecy helps believers recognize Christ in all Scripture and live in readiness for what God has promised.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 18:18-22; Isaiah 53; Micah 5:2; Amos 3:7; Luke 24:27; 2 Peter 1:20-21
RelatedPeople: Moses; Isaiah; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; Micah; Jesus
RelatedDoctrines: Prophecy; Inspiration of Scripture; Messianic Prophecy
RelatedQuestions: How can we tell true prophecy from false prophecy?; Which prophecies did Jesus fulfill?
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Jonah and Nineveh

Summary: Prophets were God's mouthpieces, speaking his word to kings and crowds whether they wanted to hear it or not. Their witness combined courage and compassion: denouncing injustice and idolatry while holding out mercy to all who would turn. The church inherits that calling: to speak truth in love, to name sin honestly, and to testify to Jesus, for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Amos; Micah; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Jonah and Nineveh

Summary: The prophets were men and women God called to speak his word into their times: Moses the lawgiver, Samuel the kingmaker, Elijah the firebrand, Isaiah the seer, and John the Baptist, the last and greatest of the old order. They comforted the afflicted and afflicted the comfortable, always pointing beyond themselves to the coming Messiah. Their books still preach, because the God who spoke through them has not stopped speaking.
RelatedPeople: Moses; Samuel; Elijah; Isaiah; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; The Burning Bush

Summary: Provision is God's care for the material needs of His creatures, from manna in the wilderness to daily bread in the Lord's Prayer. Scripture ties it to both trust and work: God provides, and His people labor, share, and steward what they receive. Provision is never promised as luxury, and it is never merely spiritual - the God who feeds ravens and clothes lilies notices what His children need and meets it, often through other people's hands.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior, and Christians ask how its findings relate to Scripture's wisdom about human nature. Much of psychology describes God's design accurately - how habits form, how trauma wounds, how relationships heal - while its theories about ultimate meaning sometimes conflict with biblical anthropology. The Christian approach is integration without surrender: receive genuine insight gratefully, test every claim against Scripture, and remember that people are souls as well as systems.

Purity is singleness of heart: a life unmixed, undivided, and set apart for God. Jesus promised that the pure in heart will see God, and the New Testament calls believers to flee impurity and to wash in the truth that makes us clean. Purity is not prudishness but wholeness: the same God who made our bodies calls us to honor him in them, by the power of the Spirit who dwells within.

Reason is the God-given capacity to think clearly, weigh evidence, and follow arguments where they lead. Christianity has always claimed that faith is not against reason: Paul reasoned in the synagogues, and the church's greatest thinkers argued that truth cannot contradict truth. Reason has limits - it cannot by itself grasp grace or resurrect the dead - but it is a servant of faith, clearing away bad arguments and helping believers love God with all their minds.

Reasoning is the practice of thinking well: forming beliefs for good reasons, spotting fallacies, and changing your mind when the evidence requires it. Scripture commends it - the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test what they heard - and warns against its counterfeits, like rationalization and cleverness in service of pride. For Christians, good reasoning is a spiritual discipline: it protects the church from error, sharpens witness, and honors a God who is Himself the Logos, the divine Reason.

Rebellion is the old human story: creatures shaking their fists at the Creator, from Eden's forbidden tree to Israel's golden calf to our own daily refusals. Scripture never softens it: rebellion brings ruin. Yet it never leaves it hopeless, for God answers rebellion with mercy, pursuing rebels until they come home. Every story of rebellion in the Bible is therefore also a story about grace that is greater than our defiance.

Rebuilding is God's repeated work among ruins: after judgment, after exile, after failure, he gathers what is broken and builds again. Nehemiah rebuilt a wall, Zerubbabel a temple, and God himself rebuilds ruined lives, raising them into a holy temple in the Lord. The Bible's rebuilding stories teach us not to despise small beginnings, for God delights to start again with what the world calls wreckage.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: Reconciliation is the restoration of a broken relationship, and in Scripture it is first God's work toward us: while we were enemies, Christ died to bring us back. That vertical reconciliation creates a horizontal one - Jew and Gentile, offender and offended, enemies made one new people - and the church is entrusted with its ministry. Reconciliation is not pretending nothing happened; it is truth, repentance, forgiveness, and rebuilt trust, in that costly order.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Prodigal Son

Summary: Redemption is God's act of buying His people back from slavery to sin at a great price. In the Old Testament God redeemed Israel from Egypt; in the New Testament Christ redeems us by His blood. The redeemed are not just forgiven, they are freed to belong to God forever.
KeyPassages: Exodus 6:6; Psalm 130:7-8; Mark 10:45; Ephesians 1:7; Colossians 1:13-14; 1 Peter 1:18-19
RelatedQuestions: What does it mean that Jesus redeemed us?; What are we redeemed from?
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Ruth; Mark; Ephesians; 1 Peter; Psalms; Romans
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Summary: Reform is the church's recurring work of returning to Scripture when tradition, power, or complacency have pulled it off course. From Josiah's rediscovered law to the Protestant Reformers' recovery of grace, reform movements share a pattern: a fresh encounter with God's Word, repentance for accumulated error, and costly resistance from those who benefit from the status quo. Reform reminds every generation that the church is always in need of renewal - and that renewal begins with repentance, not with rebranding.

The Reformation was the sixteenth-century movement that reshaped Western Christianity, sparked by Martin Luther's protest against indulgences and carried forward by reformers across Europe. Its rallying cries - Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, God's glory alone - recovered the gospel of free grace for millions and split the Western church. Its legacy is contested: renewal and division in the same event, and modern Christians inherit both the recovered truths and the responsibility to pursue unity without surrendering them.

Reformed theology is the tradition flowing from John Calvin and the Reformation, organized around God's sovereignty in salvation: grace that initiates, sustains, and completes redemption. Its landmarks include the five points of Calvinism, covenant theology, and confessions like Westminster, all emphasizing that salvation is God's work from first to last. Reformed Christians differ from other believers mainly on the mechanics of grace - election, atonement's extent, and perseverance - while sharing the same gospel of Christ crucified.
RelatedDoctrines: Election; Predestination; Perseverance of the Saints

Summary: When trouble comes, Scripture invites us to run to God as to a fortress, a shelter, a hiding place. The psalmists call him refuge in war, in grief, in guilt, and in old age: not a distant idea but a present help. To take refuge in God is to trust his character more than our circumstances, and to hide in him until the storm passes.

Regeneration is the Spirit's work of giving new spiritual life to a dead heart - the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus. It is monergistic in Reformed language: God acts first, and our faith and repentance follow as the fruit, not the cause. Regeneration is instantaneous and invisible, but its effects are visible over time: new desires, new loves, and a new direction that theologians call sanctification.

Relativism is the claim that truth, especially moral truth, depends on the individual or culture - true for you, but not for me. It feels tolerant, but it collapses under its own weight: the claim that there is no absolute truth is itself stated absolutely, and it leaves no ground to condemn real evils. Christians answer with both conviction and grace: truth is one and knowable, because it is grounded in God's character, and that conviction frees us to listen patiently rather than forcing agreement.

Remembering is a spiritual discipline in Scripture, not mere nostalgia: Israel was commanded to remember the Exodus, to retell it to their children, and to set up stones so they would not forget. Forgetting God is the first step toward idolatry; remembering his deeds is the anchor of faith in every new crisis. The Lord's Supper is remembering made tangible: bread and cup that preach the gospel to our forgetful hearts.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; The Last Supper; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Summary: Remembrance in the Bible is active: God remembers his covenant, and his people are called to remember his works, his words, and his warnings. Memorials: Passover, the stones at Gilgal, the Lord's Supper, were given because human hearts drift. To remember rightly is to live gratefully and obediently, letting yesterday's deliverances fuel today's trust.
RelatedEvents: The Passover; Crossing the Jordan; The Last Supper

Summary: Again and again God preserves a remnant: a faithful few kept through judgment: Noah's family, the seven thousand who never bowed to Baal, the exiles who returned. The remnant is proof that God's purposes never depend on majorities, and that his grace always keeps a people for himself. In the New Testament the remnant widens: Jews and Gentiles together, chosen by grace, become the one people of God.
RelatedEvents: Elijah on Mount Carmel; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Repentance is the turning of the whole person - mind, heart, and direction - away from sin and toward God. It begins with honest recognition, includes sorrow for sin itself rather than merely its consequences, and proves itself in changed behavior: Zacchaeus repaid what he stole, and John the Baptist demanded fruit worthy of repentance. Repentance is not a one-time event but the rhythm of the Christian life, and it is always met by a Father who runs to meet returning children.
KeyPassages: Psalm 51:1-17; Isaiah 55:6-7; Luke 15:11-32; Luke 19:1-10; Acts 2:37-39; 2 Corinthians 7:10
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; The Prodigal Son; David and Bathsheba

Summary: Respectful dialogue is conversation that honors the other person as made in God's image, even when you deeply disagree. Scripture models it: Jesus asked questions before He answered them, Paul reasoned rather than ridiculed in Athens, and Peter told believers to give reasons with gentleness and respect. It is not compromise - truth still matters - but it refuses contempt, straw men, and the urge to win at the cost of the relationship.

Rest is the God-given rhythm of stopping - weekly Sabbath, nightly sleep, and the deeper rest of a soul that trusts God enough to cease striving. Scripture treats rest as both command and gift: God rested after creation, Jesus invited the weary to come to Him, and Hebrews promises a Sabbath rest still to come. In a culture that measures worth by output, rest is an act of faith: it confesses that the world runs on God's power, not ours.

Restoration is God's work of bringing back what was lost or broken: Israel returned from exile, a ruined life rebuilt, and finally a whole creation made new. The prophets picture it as streams in the desert and dry bones living again, and the New Testament extends it to relationships, bodies, and the cosmos itself. Restoration is larger than repair - it is renewal with interest, the thief repaying sevenfold, the prodigal honored as a son rather than hired as a servant.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: The resurrection is God's raising of Jesus from the dead on the third day, vindicating Him as Lord and guaranteeing believers' future resurrection. It rests on the empty tomb, eyewitness testimony, and the transformed lives of the first disciples. If Christ has been raised, death is not the end and hope is anchored in fact, not wishful thinking.
KeyPassages: Matthew 28:1-10; John 20; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22; Romans 6:9; 1 Peter 1:3
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Peter; Paul; Thomas
RelatedQuestions: What evidence is there for the resurrection?; Why does the resurrection matter if Jesus already died for sins?

Summary: Jesus' resurrection is the firstfruits of the new creation, God's public declaration that death does not have the last word. Believers share that life now, raised with Christ and empowered by the Spirit to walk in newness of life. One day our bodies too will be raised, imperishable, to share His glory forever.
KeyPassages: John 11:25-26; Romans 6:4-5; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22; Philippians 3:10-11; Colossians 3:1; 1 Peter 1:3
RelatedBooks: John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; Philippians; Colossians; 1 Peter
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Lazarus; Mary Magdalene; Paul; Peter
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Raising of Lazarus; Pentecost

Summary: Return is the Bible's word for repentance: turning back from the far country to the Father, from idols to the living God. The prodigal's return is the pattern: a long walk home met by a running father. God does not merely permit return; he pleads for it, promises to receive it, and rejoices over every sinner who turns.
RelatedEvents: The Prodigal Son; The Conversion of Paul

Summary: After seventy years in Babylon, God kept his promise and brought his people home: Cyrus decreed it, Zerubbabel led it, and Ezra and Nehemiah rebuilt what exile had broken. The return was joyful yet incomplete: the people were home but still waiting for a greater deliverance. That longing points to Christ, whose return from the grave and promised return in glory will end every exile for good.
RelatedPeople: Cyrus the Great; Zerubbabel; Ezra; Nehemiah
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: The New Testament ends as it begins its hope: Jesus, who ascended, will return in glory to judge the living and the dead and to make all things new. His return is not a puzzle to solve but a promise to live by: it calls us to readiness, to holiness, and to hope that no suffering is final. Every Maranatha since the apostles has been the church's way of saying: come, Lord Jesus.

The Bible is full of reunions that picture God's heart: Jacob embracing Esau, Joseph revealing himself to his brothers, the father running to his prodigal son. Each reunion is a small resurrection: what was lost is found, what was dead is alive. The greatest reunion is still to come, when God's scattered people are gathered from every nation to one table with the Lamb.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Esau; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Jesus
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Prodigal Son

Summary: God delights in reversals: the last become first, the proud are scattered, the humble lifted, the cross becomes a throne. Hannah sang it, Mary sang it, and Jesus lived it: the stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone. Reversal is the gospel's logic: God saves by turning the world's values upside down, so that no one can boast except in the Lord.
RelatedPeople: Hannah; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Jesus; Paul

Summary: Revival is a season when God stirs His people to renewed repentance, prayer, and mission - sometimes sweeping whole regions, as in the Great Awakenings. Scripture's revivals share a pattern: rediscovered truth, conviction of sin, earnest prayer, and fruit that lasts beyond the excitement. Christians pray for revival while remembering it cannot be manufactured: methods can prepare the ground, but only the Spirit gives the increase, and true revival always shows up in changed lives and renewed churches.

Righteousness is right standing before God and right living before people - two sides of one word in Scripture. No one achieves the first by the second: God credits Christ's righteousness to believers by faith, and that gift then produces a life that increasingly does what is right. The prophets and apostles agree: righteousness is both a status received and a calling pursued, and a church that separates them has misunderstood both.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:6; Psalm 1:1-6; Isaiah 61:10; Romans 3:21-26; Romans 5:17; Philippians 3:7-9

Summary: The righteousness of God is both who he is and what he does: he is perfectly just, and he acts to make things right, vindicating the oppressed and judging the wicked. In the gospel, Paul announces something astonishing: God's righteousness is given to sinners through faith in Christ, so that the unjust are declared just. To trust in God's righteousness is to stop building our own and to rest in his finished work.

David rose from shepherd boy to king: anointed in obscurity, tested in the wilderness, crowned after years of waiting and war. His rise shows God's pattern of choosing the overlooked and preparing leaders in hidden places. Yet David's story also warns us: the king after God's own heart fell grievously, and his greater Son would be the King who never falls.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; King David; King Saul; Jonathan
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; David and Goliath

Summary: Sacraments and ordinances are the church's sacred practices: most traditions count baptism and the Lord's Supper, while Catholics and Orthodox add others. Churches differ on what to call them and how they work - means of grace, memorials, or both - but agree they were instituted by Christ and mark belonging to His people. Baptism washes into the new covenant community; the Supper feeds it at the Lord's table; both preach the gospel to the senses.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Baptism of Jesus

Summary: From the first offerings in Genesis to the Passover lamb and the daily temple sacrifices, Scripture teaches that sin costs life and that God Himself provides the substitute. All those sacrifices point forward to Jesus, the Lamb of God who offered Himself once for all. Because His sacrifice is complete, we can draw near to God with confidence.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Aaron; Jesus; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Passover; The Crucifixion

Summary: Salvation is God's rescue of sinners from sin, death, and judgment, accomplished by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. The Old Testament celebrates God as Saviour who delivers His people, and the New Testament proclaims that same salvation to all who believe. It is past, present, and future: we have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved.
KeyPassages: Exodus 14:13; Psalm 62:1; Isaiah 12:2; Luke 19:10; Acts 4:12; Ephesians 2:8-9
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; Isaiah; Luke; Acts; Ephesians
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection; Pentecost

Summary: Sanctification is the Holy Spirit's lifelong work of making believers holy in practice, growing them into the likeness of Christ. It begins at conversion, advances through obedience, trials, and the ordinary means of grace, and is completed when we see Jesus face to face. God calls us to pursue holiness while resting in the promise that He will finish what He started.
KeyPassages: John 17:17; Romans 6:22; 1 Thessalonians 4:3; 1 Thessalonians 5:23-24; Hebrews 12:14; 1 Peter 1:15-16; 1 John 3:2-3
RelatedQuestions: How do Christians grow in holiness?; Can a Christian be sanctified and still struggle with sin?

Summary: Satan is the personal, spiritual adversary Scripture calls the accuser, the tempter, and the god of this age - a fallen creature, not God's equal. He appears as the serpent in Eden, the accuser of Job, the tempter of Jesus, and the dragon of Revelation, always working by deception and accusation. Christians take him seriously without fearing him: Christ has disarmed him at the cross, and believers resist him by truth, faith, and the armor of God, knowing his defeat is certain.
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:1-15; Job 1:6-12; Matthew 4:1-11; Ephesians 6:10-18; 1 Peter 5:8-9; Revelation 12:7-12
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Job; Matthew; Ephesians; 1 Peter; Revelation
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: The good news is not for one tribe or nation: Simeon called Jesus a light for the Gentiles, the angels announced joy for all people, and Revelation pictures a multitude from every nation before the throne. God desires all people to be saved, and the church's mission flows from that breadth: a Savior for all means a gospel for all.

Science is the disciplined study of the natural world: observing, testing, and building models that predict how things work. Christians have historically led in science because their worldview expects an orderly creation made by a rational God - and because studying it is a form of worship, not a threat. Science answers how questions with power and precision; it cannot by itself answer why questions about purpose, value, or God, which is why the conflict is often between philosophies, not between science and faith.

Science and faith meet at the biggest questions: where the universe came from, why it is intelligible, and what humans are for. History shows several models - conflict, independence, dialogue, integration - and Christians hold them with different emphases, from young-earth creation to evolutionary creationism. What unites the conversation is the conviction that truth is one: if God made the world and wrote the Word, careful science and careful exegesis will not finally contradict, even where they currently seem to.
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?

Summary: Scripture is the written Word of God: sixty-six books that Christians receive as inspired, authoritative, and sufficient for faith and life. It is both human and divine - written by real authors in real cultures, yet breathed out by God - which is why Christians read it historically, literarily, and prayerfully at once. Scripture's center is Christ: the Old Testament anticipates Him, the Gospels present Him, and the Epistles explain what His coming means for the church.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:6-9; Psalm 119:97-105; Matthew 4:1-4; Luke 24:27; 2 Timothy 3:14-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Psalms; Matthew; Luke; 2 Timothy; 2 Peter

Summary: The second coming is Christ's promised return in glory to judge the living and the dead, defeat evil, and make all things new. Scripture urges believers not to speculate idly about dates but to watch, work, and encourage one another as the day approaches. His return is the blessed hope that steadies Christians in every trial.
KeyPassages: Matthew 24:30-31; John 14:1-3; Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; Titus 2:13; Revelation 22:20
RelatedDoctrines: Second Coming; Eschatology; Resurrection of the Dead; Final Judgment
RelatedQuestions: When will Jesus return?; What will happen when Jesus comes back?

Summary: Seeking God is the active pursuit of His presence, will, and face - through prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience. Scripture promises that those who seek Him will find Him, not because seeking earns His favor but because He has already turned toward us. Seeking is both a season and a posture: the desperate search of the lost, the daily discipline of the faithful, and the lifelong journey of people who have tasted and want more.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 27:8; Psalm 63:1; Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 6:33; Hebrews 11:6

Summary: The servant theme runs from Joseph and Moses through Isaiah's suffering servant to Jesus, who came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom. True greatness in God's kingdom is measured by towel and basin, not throne and title. To follow the Servant is to take the lowest place gladly, trusting that the Father sees and rewards what the world overlooks.

Greatness in God's kingdom is measured by service, a pattern set by Jesus who came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom. Isaiah's Suffering Servant, the foot-washing in John 13, and Paul's teaching all call believers to humble, joyful service. The Servant King shows us that stooping to serve is the way up in His kingdom.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 53:11; Mark 10:43-45; John 13:14-15; Philippians 2:5-8; 1 Peter 4:10
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Summary: Service is worship with its sleeves rolled up: the church's gifts are given not for display but for building others up, and Jesus made himself the model by washing feet. From deacons to door-keepers, from hosts to helpers, every act of service in Christ's name is sacred work. The New Testament measures spiritual maturity not by knowledge alone but by love that stoops to serve.

To shelter in Christ is to hide in the safest place in the universe: united to him, we are covered by his righteousness, kept by his power, and held through every storm. The psalmist's fortress and the hen's wings both point here: to a refuge that is a person, not a place. Whatever threatens, the believer can say with Paul that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

God reveals Himself as a Shepherd who seeks, feeds, guides, and protects His sheep, most tenderly in Psalm 23. Israel's leaders were meant to shepherd the flock, and when they failed, God promised to shepherd His people Himself. Jesus fulfils that promise as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep.
KeyPassages: Genesis 49:24; Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1; Ezekiel 34:11-16; John 10:11-14; 1 Peter 5:4
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion

Summary: Sin is humanity's rebellion against God, beginning with Adam and Eve and spreading to every heart, bringing death and brokenness to the world. Scripture never minimises sin, but it also never leaves us without hope. From Genesis 3:15 onward, God promises and provides a Saviour who defeats sin at the cross.
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:6-19; Psalm 51:5; Isaiah 59:2; Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23; 1 John 1:8-9
RelatedEvents: The Fall; David and Bathsheba; The Crucifixion

Summary: Sin is missing God's mark, in thought, word, and deed, and repentance is turning from it back to him, with sorrow for the sin and trust in his mercy. Scripture never separates the two: conviction without repentance hardens, and repentance without conviction is shallow. The good news is that God grants repentance as a gift, and every turning sinner finds a Father ready to forgive.

Social righteousness is God's justice lived out in public: defending the widow, feeding the hungry, freeing the oppressed, and ordering society by mercy and truth. The prophets thundered against courts that favored the rich and worship that ignored the poor, because God cares how neighbors treat neighbors.
