The church practices social righteousness when it serves its city, advocates for the vulnerable, and shows the world what God's kingdom looks like.
RelatedEvents: The Good Samaritan; The Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Son of God is the New Testament's great confession about Jesus: he is not merely a prophet or teacher but God's own Son, sharing the Father's nature and authority. The title rings out at his baptism, in Peter's confession, on the cross from a Roman centurion, and in John's Gospel from first verse to last. To call Jesus the Son of God is to worship him and to trust that in him we meet God himself.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Crucifixion

Summary: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for himself, drawn from Daniel's vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom. In Jesus the title holds both glory and suffering together: the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, came to seek and save the lost, and must be lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness. To confess him as Son of Man is to confess a King who rules by laying down his life.

The soul is the immaterial, enduring part of a human being - the seat of mind, will, and emotion that makes us more than bodies. Scripture speaks of the soul as both the whole person (a living soul) and the part that survives death, held by God until resurrection reunites it with a renewed body. Christians therefore care for souls - their own and others' - as the most valuable thing in the world, worth more than everything else combined.
KeyPassages: Genesis 2:7; Psalm 23:3; Psalm 103:1-5; Matthew 10:28; Mark 8:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:23

Summary: Sound doctrine is teaching that is healthy: true to Scripture, centered on Christ, and producing godly lives. Paul urged Timothy to hold the pattern of sound words and to guard the deposit, because what we believe shapes how we live and whom we trust. False teaching spreads like disease; sound doctrine nourishes, steadies, and protects the church.

Sovereignty is God's absolute rule over all things: nothing happens outside His knowledge, permission, or purpose. Scripture holds it together with human freedom and moral responsibility without fully resolving the tension, and it anchors comfort: if God is sovereign, suffering is never meaningless and evil never has the last word. The doctrine divides Christians on the details - how God's will relates to human choices - but unites them on the throne: the Lord reigns.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Our words reveal our hearts: Scripture warns that the tongue is a small fire able to bless or burn, and it calls us to speech that is truthful, gracious, and seasonable. James pictures the tongue as a rudder steering a whole life, while Proverbs treasures the apt word spoken at the right time. Guarding our speech is therefore not politeness but discipleship: learning to speak as people who will answer to God for every careless word.

The Holy Spirit gives every believer gifts for the common good: wisdom, teaching, encouragement, generosity, leadership, mercy, and more. Paul insists these gifts differ by design, like parts of one body, and that the greatest gift of all is love, without which every other gift is noise. Gifts are not badges of importance but tools of service, to be used humbly, eagerly, and for the building up of the church.

Spiritual warfare is the Christian's struggle against the world, the flesh, and the devil - a real conflict that is fought with spiritual weapons, not physical ones. Paul's armor of God names the equipment: truth, righteousness, gospel readiness, faith, salvation, and the Word, all wielded in prayer. The battle is already decided at the cross, yet still fiercely contested in daily life, which is why Scripture pairs vigilance with confidence: resist, stand firm, and the enemy will flee.
KeyPassages: Daniel 10:12-14; Matthew 4:1-11; Ephesians 6:10-18; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8-9; Revelation 12:7-12
RelatedBooks: Daniel; Matthew; Ephesians; James; 1 Peter; Revelation

Summary: Standing firm is holding your ground when faith is pressured: Paul told the Ephesians to put on God's armor and stand, and told the Corinthians to stand firm in the faith and be strong. Firmness is not stubbornness but rootedness: planted deep in truth, steadied by prayer, and supported by brothers and sisters who stand beside you. The one who stands firm to the end, Jesus promised, will be saved.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Daniel in the Lions' Den

Summary: Stereotypes are shortcuts the mind takes about whole groups of people - sometimes with a grain of truth, often with a load of error, always at the cost of seeing individuals. Scripture confronts them directly: Jonah's prejudice against Nineveh, the disciples' contempt for Samaritans, and James's warning against favoritism all show how group labels blind us to neighbors. The gospel answer is particular love: every person bears God's image and deserves to be known before being judged.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; The Good Samaritan; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Strength in Scripture is rarely self-sufficiency: it is God's power made perfect in human weakness, the quiet endurance of people who keep going because He keeps them. Samson had muscle and failed; Paul had a thorn and triumphed, because strength that depends on God does not run out when our own does. Christians find strength in the same places Israel did - God's promises, His people, and the honest admission that we cannot do this alone.

God's strength shows up most clearly where ours runs out: Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to go, and heard, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Weakness is therefore not the enemy of ministry but its doorway, because it forces us to lean on Christ instead of ourselves. The cross is the pattern: apparent defeat that became the world's salvation.

Suffering is the painful reality of life in a fallen world, touching every person including God's beloved people. The Bible neither minimizes pain nor offers cheap answers; it gives a suffering Savior, honest lament, and the promise that God works even affliction for good. One day God will end suffering forever, and until then He walks with His people through it.
KeyPassages: Job 38; Psalm 73; John 9:1-3; Romans 5:3-5; Romans 8:18; Romans 8:28; 2 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Peter 4:19
RelatedDoctrines: Suffering; Problem of Evil; Providence; Perseverance
RelatedQuestions: If God is good and powerful, why is there so much suffering?; Does suffering mean God is punishing me?
RelatedBooks: Job; Psalms; John; Romans; 2 Corinthians; 1 Peter

Summary: God's sufficiency is his all-enough-ness: he is enough for every need, every trial, and every calling, and his grace never runs short. Paul learned contentment in plenty and in want because he knew the God who supplies; the psalmist found that the Lord is his shepherd and therefore he lacks nothing. Sufficiency does not mean we never feel need: it means our need drives us to the One who is more than enough.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Hebrews argues from first to last that Jesus is superior: superior to angels, to Moses, to Aaron's priesthood, and to every sacrifice that came before. He is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his nature, the mediator of a better covenant with better promises. To see Christ's superiority is to stop drifting back to shadows and to hold fast to the substance who is Christ himself.

Superstition is belief in supernatural cause and effect without God's revelation to back it: lucky charms, omens, rituals that manipulate outcomes. It differs from faith because it tries to control the spiritual world rather than trust a personal God, and Scripture groups it with the occult practices Israel was told to leave behind. The cure is not cynicism but confidence: a God who speaks clearly in Scripture and acts wisely in providence leaves no need for secret signs.

Ministry has always depended on supporters: the women who funded Jesus' travels from their own means, the Philippians who partnered with Paul again and again, the churches that sent and sustained missionaries. Support, in prayer, in money, in hospitality, in encouragement, is not secondary to ministry; it IS ministry, sharing in the work and its reward. To support gospel work generously is to invest in treasure that outlasts every market.

Christ is supreme over all things: the firstborn of creation, the head of the church, the one in whom all things hold together and through whom all things will be reconciled. Colossians answers every rival power, philosophy, angel-worship, religious rules, with a single word: Christ is enough, and Christ is first. To live under his supremacy is to give him first place in everything, from our calendars to our ambitions.

Surrender is yielding our wills, plans, and very lives to God, trusting that his wisdom is better than our control. Mary answered the angel, Let it be to me according to your word; Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, Not my will, but yours. Surrender is not defeat but freedom: the daily laying down of our crowns before the King who gave himself for us.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion

Summary: Technology is every tool humans make to extend their reach, from plows to smartphones, and Scripture treats tools as morally loaded: useful for good, dangerous when they master us. The Bible's wisdom applies directly - stewardship over addiction, truth over misinformation, presence over distraction, and Sabbath over the endless scroll. Christians neither fear technology nor worship it; they ask of each new tool whether it helps them love God and neighbor better.

The temple was the dwelling place of God's presence among Israel, the centre of worship, sacrifice, and prayer in Jerusalem. Jesus honoured the temple, cleansed it, and foretold its destruction, while pointing to His own body as the true temple. Now God's Spirit dwells in His church and in every believer, and the new creation needs no temple because the Lord Himself is there.
KeyPassages: Exodus 25:8; 1 Kings 8:27-30; Psalm 84:1-4; John 2:19-21; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Revelation 21:22
RelatedBooks: Exodus; 1 Kings; Psalms; John; 1 Corinthians; Revelation
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; Pentecost; Rebuilding of the Temple

Summary: After exile, God stirred Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the returned remnant to rebuild his house in Jerusalem, and later Nehemiah to rebuild its wall. The work faced opposition, delay, and discouragement, yet God promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former. The rebuilt temple pointed forward to Christ, in whom God dwells with his people, and to the church as his living temple.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Temptation is the pull toward sin, and Scripture is honest about its universality: even Jesus was tempted, though without sin. Temptation itself is not sin - sin enters when we entertain and yield - and God promises both understanding and a way out, since no temptation is unique to us. The practical defenses are ancient: know Scripture, know your weaknesses, avoid the near occasions, confess quickly, and never fight alone.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Testimony is telling what God has done, in your life and in history, as evidence for the gospel. The New Testament treats ordinary believers' stories as powerful witness: the healed demoniac sent home to tell his friends, the Samaritan woman bringing her town to Jesus. Good testimony is specific, honest about the before and after, and centered on Christ rather than on the speaker - less look at me and more look at what the Lord has done.
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?

Summary: The Fall is humanity's first rebellion in Eden, when Adam and Eve disobeyed God, believed the serpent's lie, and brought sin, shame, and death into the world. Its effects reach every person and every part of creation. Yet even in judgment God clothed the couple, promised a serpent-crushing offspring, and began His rescue plan.
RelatedQuestions: What happened at the Fall?; Why did God allow Adam and Eve to sin?

Summary: The universe is everything that exists physically: galaxies, stars, planets, and the space and time that contain them. Modern cosmology describes a universe with a beginning, fine-tuned constants, and laws that make science possible - facts Christians read as consistent with a Creator, though not proof of one by themselves. The biblical claim is larger than any theory: the universe is not eternal or self-explaining, but spoken into being by a God who entered it.

Theology is the study of God: what He is like, what He has done, and what He asks of us, drawn from Scripture and organized for understanding. It is not an academic luxury but a practical necessity - everyone is a theologian, because everyone lives by some picture of God, accurate or not. Good theology humbles as much as it informs: it ends, as Paul's does, in worship, because the God it studies is greater than every system built to describe Him.

Time is God's gift and God's stewardship: brief as a breath, yet long enough to know him, love our neighbors, and finish the work he gives. Scripture urges us to number our days, to redeem the time, and to remember that there is a season for everything under heaven. Eternity gives time its weight: because forever is real, today matters more, not less.

Tithing is giving the first tenth to God, a practice that taught Israel to trust the Lord as provider and to fund the work of worship and the care of the poor. Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek and Jacob vowed one long before the law commanded it. Under the new covenant, the tenth remains a wise starting point, but the deeper principle is larger still: generous, cheerful, firstfruits giving from hearts that know everything belongs to God.

Tradition is the church's handed-down faith: creeds, liturgies, interpretations, and practices passed from generation to generation. Scripture treats tradition with both respect and suspicion - Paul tells churches to hold to what was delivered, while Jesus rebukes traditions that nullify God's commands. The Reformation's rule remains the test: tradition is a faithful servant when it carries Scripture forward, and a tyrant when it replaces it.

Transformation is the gradual remaking of a person into Christ's likeness, the New Testament's word for what happens after conversion. It is not self-improvement by willpower but renewal by the Spirit: beholding Christ, renewing the mind, and practicing new patterns until they become character. Transformation is slow, uneven, and communal - it happens as we worship, confess, forgive, and serve - and its proof is not perfection but direction: more love, more honesty, more peace than before.

Translation is rendering Scripture from Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek into the languages people actually speak - work the church has done since the Septuagint, three centuries before Christ. Every translation involves interpretation, which is why Christians use several and compare them, and why new translations keep appearing as language changes and manuscripts improve. The doctrine beneath it is confidence: God's Word can be faithfully carried across languages, because its Author intends to be understood.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: The Trinity is the biblical teaching that God is one in essence and three in person: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Each person is fully God, yet there is only one God, a mystery Scripture affirms from creation to Christ's baptism to the Great Commission. Knowing God as Trinity shapes how Christians pray, worship, and understand love itself.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:26; Deuteronomy 6:4; Matthew 3:16-17; Matthew 28:19; John 1:1-3; 2 Corinthians 13:14
RelatedDoctrines: Trinity; God the Father; Christology; Holy Spirit
RelatedQuestions: Is the Trinity taught in the Bible?; How can God be three and one at the same time?

Summary: True worship is the whole-life response to God's worth: not only songs on Sunday but obedience on Monday, offered in spirit and truth. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the Father seeks worshipers who worship this way, and the prophets insisted that ritual without justice is noise to God. True worship therefore has two tests: is it directed to the true God, and does it change how we live toward our neighbor?
RelatedQuestions: What is true worship according to the Bible?

Summary: Trust is reliance on God's character when circumstances argue otherwise - the practical shape of faith. Proverbs warns against leaning on our own understanding, the Psalms model trust as refuge-taking, and Jesus sleeps in a storm His disciples fear, showing what trust looks like embodied. Trust grows the way all trust grows: through kept promises remembered, through small obediences, and through suffering that proves God faithful when nothing else holds.
RelatedQuestions: What should I do when my faith feels weak?

Summary: Truth is what corresponds to reality, and in Scripture it is ultimately personal: Jesus calls Himself the truth, and God's Word is described as truth itself. That makes truth-telling a moral duty and truth-seeking a spiritual one - Christians do not get to invent their own facts, and they do not get to hide behind relativism when the truth is costly. The church's witness depends on it: a gospel proclaimed with lies, exaggerations, or half-truths undermines the very message it carries.
KeyPassages: Psalm 119:160; John 1:14; John 8:31-32; John 14:6; John 18:37; Ephesians 4:15

Summary: Unfaithfulness is breaking trust with God: Israel's idolatry is pictured as adultery, and Hosea's marriage became a living parable of a people who kept wandering from their faithful Husband. Scripture names unfaithfulness plainly because it wounds real relationship. Yet it never ends there, for God remains faithful even when we are faithless, and calls his people back with cords of love.

Unity is the church's witness: Jesus prayed that his people would be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world would believe. Paul pleaded for one mind, one Spirit, one body: not uniformity, for gifts differ, but a deep oneness rooted in one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Unity is kept by humility, gentleness, and forgiveness, and it is broken most often by pride.

Unity in Christ is deeper than agreement: in him, Jew and Gentile, slave and free, male and female are one people, reconciled to God and to each other by one cross. The dividing wall is broken down, and former strangers become fellow citizens and members of God's household. To live this unity is to refuse every identity that competes with Christ and to love across every line the world draws.

Urgency runs through the gospel: now is the day of salvation, the night is far gone, the harvest is plentiful and the workers are few. Jesus warned against the rich fool who planned for tomorrow and lost today, and Paul pleaded with people to be reconciled to God without delay. Urgency is not panic but holy seriousness: living as people who know time is short and eternity is long.

Vanity is the emptiness Ecclesiastes names: chasing wealth, pleasure, wisdom, or fame apart from God leaves the hands full of wind. The Preacher tried everything and found it vapor: beautiful, brief, and unable to satisfy. Vanity is not a counsel of despair but a diagnosis: only when we stop expecting the world to give us meaning can we receive life as God's gift and enjoy it without worshipping it.

Victory in Scripture is won, not earned: Israel's battles were God's before they were theirs, and the decisive victory over sin and death belongs to Christ alone. Christians share in it by faith, which is why Paul can call suffering believers more than conquerors in the middle of hardship rather than after it. Victory therefore looks different from triumph: it is endurance, forgiveness, and faithfulness that hold the field because the war's outcome is already settled.
KeyPassages: Exodus 14:13-14; 1 Samuel 17:45-47; John 16:33; Romans 8:35-39; 1 Corinthians 15:54-57; 1 John 5:4-5
RelatedBooks: Exodus; 1 Samuel; John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; 1 John
RelatedEvents: David and Goliath; The Walls of Jericho; The Resurrection

Summary: Christ's victory was won where defeat seemed certain: on the cross he disarmed the powers, in the tomb he broke death's grip, and in his resurrection he announced that the war is over even while battles remain. Believers share that victory now, over sin, over fear, over the accuser, and will see it complete when he returns. To live in his victory is to fight from triumph, not for it.

In the Old Testament, Israel is God's vine, planted to bear fruit for the nations, yet often failing to do so. Jesus takes up the image, declaring Himself the true Vine and His disciples the branches who bear fruit only by abiding in Him. Fruitfulness flows from remaining in Christ, not from striving apart from Him.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Last Supper; Pentecost

Summary: Violence in Scripture is a hard problem Christians must face honestly: the Old Testament contains wars commanded by God, and the New Testament reveals a Savior who absorbs violence rather than inflicting it. Interpreters differ on how to hold these together - some stress progressive revelation, others divine judgment, others the ancient context - but all orthodox readings agree on the trajectory: a world broken by violence, a cross that ends its cycle, and a kingdom where swords become plowshares.
KeyPassages: Genesis 6:11-13; Joshua 6:1-27; Psalm 46:8-10; Matthew 5:38-48; Isaiah 2:2-4; Revelation 21:1-4
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Joshua; Psalms; Matthew; Isaiah; Revelation

Summary: Visions are one way God has spoken: Jacob's ladder, Isaiah's throne room, Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, John's apocalypse. They come in pictures because some truths are too large for plain prose, and they always serve God's purposes: calling, comforting, or commissioning his people. Visions must be tested by Scripture and by their fruit, for not every dazzling sight is from God, but the true ones have steadied his people for millennia.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Isaiah; Ezekiel; John the Apostle

Summary: Waiting on God is active trust, not passive resignation: the psalmist waits more than watchmen for the morning, Isaiah promises new strength to those who wait, and the church waited ten days in prayer before Pentecost. Waiting purifies our motives, deepens our dependence, and teaches us that God's timing is part of his goodness. Those who wait on the Lord will not be put to shame.

Wandering and return is the shape of Israel's story and of every human heart: God's people strayed into the wilderness, into exile, into idolatry, and God kept bringing them back. The wilderness wanderings taught dependence, the exile taught humility, and every return taught grace. Our own wanderings need not end in ruin, because the God who sought Israel still seeks wanderers today.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Prodigal Son; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Water appears at creation, in the Flood, at the Red Sea, and in water from the rock, as a picture of both judgment and life-giving salvation. The prophets promised cleansing water and rivers in the desert, and Jesus offered living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. Baptism unites believers with Christ, and Revelation ends with the river of the water of life.
KeyPassages: Genesis 1:2; Exodus 14:21-31; Exodus 17:6; Ezekiel 36:25; John 4:13-14; John 7:37-39; Revelation 22:1-2
RelatedPeople: Moses; Noah; Jesus; The Samaritan Woman
RelatedEvents: Creation; Noah and the Flood; The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Baptism of Jesus
Places: Garden of Eden; Mount Ararat; Egypt; Jordan River

Summary: Weakness is the human condition Scripture refuses to romanticize or despise: we are frail, limited, and dependent, and God meets us there rather than waiting for us to get strong. Paul's thorn taught him that grace is sufficient precisely where strength fails, and the church's strength has always come from admitting need rather than hiding it. Weakness is therefore not the opposite of faith but often its clearest evidence: trust is easiest to see when there is nothing else to lean on.

The wilderness is where God forms his people: Israel wandered there forty years, Elijah fled there in despair, and Jesus was tested there before his ministry began. It is a place of hunger and danger, but also of manna, of water from the rock, and of God's voice in the silence. No one chooses the wilderness, yet Scripture insists that God meets us there, and leads us out, humbled, fed, and ready.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; The Temptation in the Wilderness
Places: Mount Sinai; Kadesh Barnea; Plains of Moab

Summary: Biblical wisdom is skill in living well under God's rule, beginning with the fear of the Lord. Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes teach that wisdom is found not in cleverness but in trusting God, listening to counsel, and walking humbly. Jesus is presented as wisdom itself, greater than Solomon, calling us to build our lives on His words.
KeyPassages: Job 28:28; Psalm 90:12; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 3:5-6; Ecclesiastes 12:13; Matthew 7:24; 1 Corinthians 1:30; James 3:17
RelatedDoctrines: Wisdom; Fear of the Lord; Providence
RelatedQuestions: What is biblical wisdom and how do I get it?; Why does the book of Ecclesiastes sound so pessimistic?
RelatedBooks: Job; Psalms; Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; James; 1 Corinthians
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple; The Birth of Jesus

Summary: Witness is the church's calling to testify to what God has done, in words and in life. The legal metaphor is deliberate: witnesses do not invent the case, they report what they have seen and heard, and the Spirit makes the testimony effective. Witness takes many forms - a shared story, a defended hope, a life that makes the gospel plausible - but its center is always Jesus: His death, resurrection, and the new life He gives.
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?

Summary: The Word of God is God's self-revelation: Christ Himself, the living Word, and Scripture, the written Word that testifies to Him. Christians distinguish the two without separating them - the written Word's authority flows from the living Word it proclaims. To call the Bible God's Word is to claim it speaks with His voice: it creates, convicts, comforts, and commands, and it stands as the church's final court of appeal.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: Word studies are the careful examination of biblical words in their original languages, tracing how Hebrew and Greek terms are used across Scripture. Done well, they unlock precision - the difference between kinds of love, or what covenant meant to its first hearers - and done badly, they mislead, as when a word's root is mistaken for its meaning. Word studies serve the church best when they stay humble: words get their meaning from sentences, sentences from books, and books from the whole canon.

Works in Scripture are both warned against and commanded: we are not saved by works, yet we are saved for good works, created in Christ Jesus to walk in them. Paul and James agree: faith without works is dead, and works without faith are empty. Good works are therefore not the price of salvation but its fruit: the visible life of a people already loved, already forgiven, already free.

World religions are the great faith traditions alongside Christianity - Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and others - each with its own scriptures, practices, and picture of ultimate reality. Christians approach them with both respect and conviction: respect for the people who hold them and the truths they contain, and conviction that Jesus Christ is the unique Son of God and the only Savior. Understanding other faiths fairly matters for honest witness, good neighboring, and answering the question of why Christians believe what they do.

A worldview is the set of assumptions through which a person interprets everything: what is real, what is true, what is right, and what humans are for. Everyone has one, whether examined or not, and the Christian worldview - creation, fall, redemption, restoration - offers a coherent alternative to naturalism, pantheism, and relativism. Christians study worldviews to understand their neighbors, to test their own thinking, and to show how the gospel answers the deepest questions every worldview must face.

Worship is the believer's whole-life response to who God is and what He has done, expressed in song, prayer, obedience, and awe. True worship is in spirit and truth, centered on God's worth rather than our preferences. From the tabernacle to the throne room of heaven, worship is both our duty and our delight.
KeyPassages: Exodus 20:3; Psalm 95:6; Psalm 100; John 4:23-24; Romans 12:1; Hebrews 12:28; Revelation 5:12-13
RelatedPeople: David; Asaph; Jesus; Paul; John; Abraham
RelatedQuestions: What is true worship according to the Bible?; Why does God want our worship?
RelatedBooks: Exodus; Psalms; John; Romans; Revelation; Genesis
